TITLE: Learnability-Gated Token Depth: Reallocate Layers to Informative Tokens

MECHANISM: Insert a frozen-ish shallow "probe head" at ~40% depth whose per-token loss is compared to the full-model loss from the previous epoch/step-window, yielding a cheap online "residual learnability" score; tokens already predicted well by the shallow probe skip the upper transformer blocks (straight-through residual passthrough), and the freed FLOPs are spent on drawing extra high-learnability tokens into the same fixed token-budget batch. Data efficiency improves because gradient signal concentrates on tokens with nonzero remaining learnable structure instead of memorized boilerplate; compute efficiency improves because skipped tokens cost ~40% of a full forward-backward; energy efficiency improves superlinearly because skipping is contiguous in depth (whole blocks unexecuted, not masked), so it cuts DRAM traffic and activation memory rather than just nominal FLOPs. Unlike curriculum or data pruning, nothing is discarded at the document level — easy tokens still contribute shallow-path loss, so no distributional collapse and no compute-for-data trade.

TEST: Train 150M-param models on 4B tokens of FineWeb-Edu at matched wall-clock and matched measured joules (RAPL/NVML), comparing baseline dense training vs. learnability-gated depth; falsified if gated runs fail to beat baseline validation loss at equal energy *and* equal token count simultaneously.

TITLE: Ghost Steps: Free Quasi-Newton Iterations Inside a Gradient Sketch Subspace

MECHANISM: Maintain a rank-r (r≈32) orthonormal sketch of recent minibatch gradients plus the secant pairs (Δw, Δg) already produced by ordinary training, and fit an exact r×r quadratic model of the loss restricted to that subspace. After each real forward/backward pass, take several "ghost" optimizer steps that use the *model's predicted* gradient inside the subspace rather than a new batch — each ghost step costs O(r²) plus one rank-r weight update, with zero activation memory traffic and no new tokens. This extracts second-order information that the run already paid for but normally discards, so every token purchases more optimization progress (data efficiency), fewer real passes are needed to reach a target loss (compute efficiency), and because ghost steps touch no activations or HBM-resident intermediates they consume near-zero incremental joules, making the energy gain strictly larger than the FLOP gain. Trust-region clipping on the subspace step size, refreshed whenever the sketch's predicted-vs-actual gradient residual exceeds a threshold, keeps the local quadratic model honest and prevents the usual subspace-overfitting failure.

TEST: Train a 100M-parameter model twice at identical token budget and hyperparameters, with and without ghost steps, and check whether loss-versus-tokens improves while measured joules-to-target-loss also drops — if the loss-versus-tokens curve is unchanged or worse, the mechanism is dead.

TITLE: Quorum-Gated Sparse Backpropagation via Trimmed-Consensus Token Updates

MECHANISM: In each step, the existing data-parallel replicas (each already at slightly different parameter states from staleness/EMA offsets and different dropout masks) each produce a cheap per-token gradient proxy — the sign of the last-layer logit-error projected onto a fixed low-dimensional random sketch — which is exchanged in a few bytes per token. A token is admitted to the backward pass only if a supermajority of replicas agree on the sketch's sign pattern; disagreeing tokens (label noise, ambiguous or already-memorized text, adversarial/duplicated junk) are dropped, and surviving per-parameter updates are combined with a coordinate-wise trimmed mean instead of a plain average. This attacks all three axes with one knob: dropping ~30–50% of tokens removes most of the backward FLOPs (≈2/3 of step cost) for those tokens, the sketch-sign exchange plus trimmed-mean replaces a full high-precision gradient all-reduce with far less interconnect traffic (the dominant non-FLOP energy term at scale), and the consensus filter raises loss-per-token by spending the budget only on updates that multiple independent views certify as genuine signal rather than noise. Crucially the gate is *not* a loss-magnitude heuristic (which keeps noisy outliers) but an agreement heuristic, so it removes exactly the updates that cancel out across replicas and thus waste energy without moving the model.

TEST: Train two 150M-parameter models on identical 3B-token web data under a matched wall-clock/joule budget — baseline all-reduce versus quorum-gated sparse backward with 4 replicas — and check whether the gated run's validation perplexity is strictly better; if it is equal or worse at matched energy, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Learnability-gated sparse backward: token-level backprop pruning with reference-model scoring

MECHANISM: During each step, run the normal forward pass, then score every token by "learnability" = current per-token loss minus the same token's loss under a cheap EMA-averaged snapshot of the model (free to obtain by reusing the forward activations of a single extra low-precision pass amortized over K steps). Tokens that are already mastered (low current loss) or hopelessly noisy (high loss, no improvement vs. snapshot) get their output-layer gradients zeroed, so backward through every MLP block and the unembedding is executed only on the surviving top-p fraction of positions, while attention backward stays dense to preserve sequence mixing. Data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on the frontier of what the model is currently learning rather than on trivially predictable filler; compute efficiency improves because MLP+unembedding backward is roughly half of total training FLOPs and scales linearly with kept tokens; energy efficiency improves superlinearly with compute because the pruned tokens' MLP activations never need to be written to or re-read from HBM, cutting the memory traffic that dominates joules-per-FLOP on modern accelerators. Crucially nothing is discarded at the data level — every token still contributes a forward pass and full attention context, so the "skipped" tokens remain available as context and can be re-selected later as the model's competence shifts.

TEST: Train two 150M-parameter models on identical 4B-token streams — baseline vs. p=0.5 learnability-gated backward — and check whether the gated run reaches the same validation loss at both fewer tokens and lower wall-clock energy measured by on-device power telemetry; if it needs more tokens, or saves FLOPs but not measured joules, the idea is dead.

TITLE: LZ-factorized training: pay compute only for novel substrings

MECHANISM: Preprocess the corpus with a suffix-automaton/LZ77 factorization so every sequence is expressed as a sequence of maximal substrings already seen plus genuinely novel factors, and cache a compact low-rank sketch of each repeated factor's hidden states keyed by its factor ID. During training, the forward/backward pass runs at full cost only over novel factors; repeated factors are injected as cached state sketches (refreshed lazily when staleness exceeds a threshold), with their multiplicity passed as an explicit count feature plus a cheap count-weighted distillation term so frequency statistics are preserved without being paid for in FLOPs. Compute and energy drop because the ~30–50% of long-substring redundancy in natural corpora is amortized to near-zero joules and to far fewer HBM round trips, while data efficiency rises because gradient budget is reallocated toward rare, novel content rather than being spent re-learning boilerplate — the model sees the full distribution but is only charged for its novelty.

TEST: Take a 100M-param model mid-training, substitute cached hidden states from checkpoints 500/2k/10k steps stale for the recomputed states of repeated factors, and measure the resulting next-token loss delta on novel spans — if staleness-induced loss degradation exceeds the loss the saved FLOPs would have bought at matched joules, the idea is dead before any full run.

TITLE: Fused Co-Resident Auxiliary Heads: Recycling Activations For Dense Supervision

MECHANISM: In a training step the joules are dominated not by multiply-accumulates but by moving activations and weights between HBM and on-chip SRAM, so any learning signal extracted from bytes *already resident on-chip* is nearly energy-free. I propose attaching a tiny (<2% params) auxiliary predictor at every few blocks, kernel-fused into the host block so it reads the block's activations from SRAM before they are written back, and emitting dense self-supervised targets (multi-token-ahead prediction plus reconstruction of the next block's pre-activation summary) whose gradients flow into the host trunk. The exchange is mutual and closed-loop: the trunk supplies representations the small predictors cannot build alone, and the predictors return per-depth gradient signal that would otherwise only arrive via the single output loss, so each token yields several distinct learning constraints instead of one. This should move all three axes together — more learning per token (data), more learning per FLOP already spent on the forward pass (compute), and amortized memory traffic per unit of loss reduction (energy) — with the caveat that oversized auxiliaries begin consuming trunk capacity and the benefit collapses, predicting an optimal small parameter share.

TEST: Train ~150M-param models on a fixed token budget with and without the fused auxiliaries, measuring wall-clock and socket-level joules, and falsify if validation loss at *equal measured joules* is not lower for the augmented model at any auxiliary size between 0.5% and 4% of parameters.
lens: Argue from energy and physics first.

TITLE: Mid-Depth Learnability Gating: drop unlearnable tokens before deep layers

MECHANISM: All tokens pass through the first k of L transformer layers; a cheap linear early-exit head there produces a per-token predicted-loss-reduction score (calibrated against the actual residual loss of the previous checkpoint), and only the top-ρ fraction of tokens are routed through the remaining L−k layers and included in the backward pass, with the rest supervised solely by the early-exit head. Unlike RHO-1-style data selection, the gate is inside the network, so skipping a token removes ~(1−k/L) of its forward FLOPs, all of its deep-layer backward FLOPs, and the associated HBM traffic and optimizer-state reads — the dominant energy term on modern accelerators. Data efficiency improves because deep-layer gradient signal concentrates on high-learnability tokens (already-memorized boilerplate and irreducible-entropy noise are excluded), compute efficiency improves because per-token FLOPs fall while the *retained* tokens are the ones that move the loss, and energy improves super-linearly relative to FLOPs because deep-layer activations shrink and shorten the sequence dimension that drives attention memory traffic. The three gains share one mechanism rather than trading against each other, since the discarded computation and the discarded learning signal are the same set of tokens.

TEST: Train 160M-param models on 6B tokens of FineWeb-Edu with k=L/2, ρ∈{0.4,0.7,1.0}, and compare validation loss at matched measured wall-clock joules (nvidia-smi integration) — falsified if no ρ<1 setting beats the ρ=1 baseline on loss-per-joule *and* loss-per-token simultaneously.

TITLE: Surprisal-Priced Precision: Matching Mantissa Bits to Token Information

MECHANISM: A frozen, near-free predictor (a hashed 5-gram plus a 2-layer proxy net) emits a prior distribution for every position before the main model runs; the main transformer is trained to predict only the *residual* logits between that prior and the truth, and each token's per-layer arithmetic precision and active depth are set proportional to its prior surprisal, so a token costing 0.3 nats gets 3-4 mantissa bits and two layers while a 9-nat token gets full bf16 and full depth. The key claim is that gradient signal-to-noise per token scales with residual entropy, so rounding noise that is small relative to a token's own information content is free — you can spend arithmetic bits like you spend nats. Data efficiency improves because capacity and gradient mass stop being consumed by the ~60% of tokens that an n-gram already nails, concentrating updates on genuinely novel structure; compute efficiency improves through the surprisal-gated depth skipping; energy efficiency improves *super-linearly* beyond the FLOP savings because multiplier energy scales roughly quadratically in mantissa width and DRAM/SRAM traffic scales linearly in bit-width, so the same FLOP count costs far fewer joules. Crucially none of the three is traded for another: the pricing rule is a single shared quantity (nats) rather than separate knobs, so the budget that saves energy is the same one that removes redundant gradient steps.

TEST: Train a 160M-param model on 4B tokens against a dense bf16 baseline with identical token budget and measure val loss versus wall-clock, FLOPs, and wall-socket joules — the idea is dead if matching baseline loss requires either more tokens or more than ~70% of baseline energy.

TITLE: Dual-Ledger Token Auditing: Reconciliation Residuals Allocate Backward Compute

MECHANISM: Standard training assumes every token in a batch deserves one loss entry and a full backward pass; instead, each token is recorded twice — once by the main next-token head, and once by a cheap auxiliary head reading a disjoint view (e.g., a low-rank shadow projection of the same trunk activations plus a right-context infilling signal) — and the two entries are required to agree under a per-token balance constraint. The signed reconciliation residual between the two accounts is a nearly free, self-generated audit statistic: tokens whose accounts balance are already consistently explained and are dropped from the backward pass, while unbalanced tokens (genuine model error, not just high entropy from irreducible ambiguity) receive full gradients plus an explicit balance penalty that ties the two heads together. Data efficiency improves because the residual is a sharper curriculum signal than loss — it separates reducible error from aleatoric noise without a separate reference or proxy model — and compute/energy improve simultaneously because the backward pass (≈2/3 of training FLOPs and the dominant memory-traffic/joule cost) is executed on a small token subset while the audit itself is forward-only and low-rank, so all three axes move together rather than trading off.

TEST: Train a 150M-parameter model on a fixed token budget under matched joules (measured, not estimated) against (a) a dense baseline and (b) identical backward-sparsity gating driven by random token selection and by plain loss magnitude — the idea is falsified if the dual-ledger residual gating fails to dominate all three on the loss-versus-joules and loss-versus-tokens curves at once.

TITLE: Learnability-gated per-token depth routing using a cheap reference model

MECHANISM: A small frozen reference model (≤1% of main-model FLOPs) scores every token in a batch by "learnability" = reference surprisal minus current-model surprisal (estimated from the previous epoch's cached logits, so no extra forward pass). Tokens in the low-learnability tails — already-mastered boilerplate and irreducible noise — are routed through only the bottom k of N transformer blocks and excluded from the loss, while high-learnability tokens get full depth; the router is a hard threshold, not learned, so it adds no parameters and no instability. This hits all three axes simultaneously rather than trading them: data efficiency improves because gradient mass concentrates on tokens with nonzero reducible loss, compute efficiency improves because skipped tokens cost a fraction of a full forward/backward, and energy falls roughly in proportion to FLOPs plus a bonus from shorter effective sequences in the upper blocks (less attention memory traffic, which dominates joule-per-token on modern accelerators). The key claim is that the same signal that identifies *what to learn from* also identifies *what not to spend depth on*, so one mechanism buys both, unlike curriculum methods that pay a scoring-forward-pass tax.

TEST: Train 150M-param models on 6B tokens of FineWeb-Edu under a fixed wall-clock/energy budget (measured via NVML) comparing (a) dense baseline, (b) loss-masking only, (c) depth-routing only, (d) both — if (d) fails to Pareto-dominate (a) on validation perplexity at equal measured joules, the joint claim is falsified.

TITLE: Surprisal-gated per-token arithmetic precision during training

MECHANISM: Each token's activation row carries an online-estimated surprisal (from the model's own running loss on that token, cheaply available from the previous microstep), and this gates which numerical precision its row is computed in: low-surprisal rows are routed to an FP4/INT4 GEMM, high-surprisal rows to BF16, with the two row-blocks executed as a single batched split-GEMM so hardware utilization stays high. Energy falls directly because MAC and memory-traffic energy scale super-linearly with bit-width and the majority of tokens in any web corpus are low-surprisal boilerplate; compute falls because low-precision tensor-core throughput is 2-4x and activation/gradient memory shrinks correspondingly. Data efficiency should *improve* rather than degrade, because quantization noise on easy tokens acts as a targeted regularizer that suppresses memorization of predictable filler while preserving full-precision gradient fidelity exactly where the model is still learning — an implicit curriculum implemented in the number system rather than in the data sampler. Crucially, nothing is thrown away: every token still contributes a gradient, so this is not token dropping and does not reduce the effective corpus.

TEST: Train two 120M-parameter models on identical 3B-token streams, one in BF16 and one with simulated per-token precision gating (stochastic-rounding quantization noise injected on rows below a surprisal percentile, no custom kernels needed), and check whether the gated run's loss-vs-tokens curve is at least as good as baseline — if it is measurably worse at matched tokens, the data-efficiency leg fails and the idea is dead.

TITLE: Criticality-Pinned Training: Gradient-Susceptibility Control of Batch, Depth, and Rate

MECHANISM: Define a cheap online order parameter — the mean pairwise cosine alignment of per-microbatch gradients — and its variance-based sensitivity to perturbations in learning rate and batch size, computed from statistics already materialized during gradient accumulation (no extra backward passes). Empirically this sensitivity is sharply peaked: below the peak the batch gradient is noise-dominated and tokens are wasted, above it microbatch gradients are redundant and the extra samples and FLOPs buy nothing. A controller continuously pins training at this peak by co-adjusting three knobs that are usually tuned independently and offline: batch size, learning rate, and the active-layer fraction under stochastic-depth / mixture-of-depths routing, shrinking all three when alignment is redundant and growing them when it is noisy. Because redundancy and noise are both wasted work, removing them cuts tokens consumed (data), FLOPs per step (compute), and wall-clock accelerator-seconds and HBM traffic (energy) simultaneously rather than trading them, since the controller never spends more of any resource than the measured marginal information gain justifies.

TEST: Train 150M-parameter models on a fixed 5B-token corpus and check whether the measured alignment-sensitivity peak actually tracks the empirical maximum of loss-reduction-per-FLOP within a run — if the peak is flat, drifts, or is uncorrelated with marginal loss reduction, the controller has no signal and the idea dies for under 200 GPU-hours.

TITLE: Learnability-gated per-token backward sparsity in position-wise blocks

MECHANISM: Keep the forward pass dense (attention needs all positions), but during backward, route gradients through only the top-k% of token positions ranked by an online "learnability" score — current per-token loss minus its EMA over recent occurrences of that token's context bucket — with importance weights restoring an unbiased estimate of the MLP weight gradient. Because MLP/position-wise blocks are ~2/3 of parameters and their weight gradient is a plain sum over token positions, dropping positions is exact subsampling rather than an approximation, cutting backward FLOPs and activation memory traffic (the dominant energy term) at k≈30%. Data efficiency improves because the gradient budget concentrates on tokens that are currently neither memorized nor noise-saturated, so each token seen yields more loss reduction; compute efficiency improves because step cost falls ~25–30% while per-step progress does not; energy efficiency improves superlinearly since skipped positions also skip activation reads/writes and allow shorter optimizer-bound stalls. The key claim is that this is not a trade: the discarded tokens are precisely those whose gradient contribution is near-zero or pure-noise, so removing them reduces cost *and* variance simultaneously.

TEST: Train 160M-param models on 4B tokens of FineWeb-Edu with k∈{100%, 50%, 30%} and compare validation loss at both matched-tokens and matched-FLOPs — if k=30% is not strictly better than dense on the matched-FLOPs curve while staying within noise on matched-tokens, the joint-frontier claim is false.

TITLE: Near-Duplicate Batching: Shared Prefixes as Gradient Control Variates

MECHANISM: Instead of deduplicating web text (which discards data), cluster near-duplicate documents by cheap MinHash and build each minibatch from k-tuples that share a long common prefix, training on their divergent continuations. The shared prefix is forward- and backward-computed once and structurally reused across the tuple (one KV/activation trunk, k heads), cutting both FLOPs and — more importantly for joules — per-token HBM traffic, which dominates training energy. Simultaneously, the matched tuples act as common-random-number control variates: subtracting the tuple-mean gradient isolates the *contrastive* signal between texts that differ only where they are informative, lowering gradient noise scale so fewer optimizer steps and fewer unique tokens reach a target loss. All three axes improve from one mechanism because duplicate structure is being spent as compute-sharing *and* variance reduction rather than deleted as redundancy.

TEST: Train a 100M-param model on ~2B tokens with k=4 prefix-shared duplicate tuples versus standard dedup + random batching, and check whether loss-vs-unique-tokens, loss-vs-FLOPs, and measured gradient noise scale all improve — if any one regresses, or prefix-clustering overhead exceeds the trunk-sharing savings, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Affinity-Gated Clonal Adapters: Sparse Selection, Local Mutation, Mastery-Based Data Retirement

MECHANISM: Attach a large pool of tiny low-rank adapter "clones" to each block; per microbatch, a cheap sketched gradient-alignment score selects only the top-k clones, and forward/backward/optimizer state are computed for those alone, so active parameters and HBM traffic per token fall sharply. Clones that repeatedly win on a data cluster are duplicated-with-perturbation and refined only within their own low-rank subspace (localized mutation), while persistently losing or held-out-harming clones are pruned, concentrating capacity where the model is still failing. A running per-cluster competence estimate retires mastered data to a low replay rate, so fresh tokens are spent only on regions with unresolved loss rather than re-deriving what a specialist already encodes. Data efficiency comes from spending samples only on unmastered clusters, compute efficiency from top-k sparse updates, and energy efficiency from the reduced optimizer state and memory movement that those two changes jointly imply — none is traded for the others because all three reductions stem from the same selection signal.

TEST: Train a 150M-parameter model on ~10B tokens and plot validation loss against measured joules and against tokens consumed; the idea is falsified if the clonal-selection run fails to dominate an energy-matched and token-matched dense baseline on both curves simultaneously.

TITLE: Gradient-Gated Backpropagation: token-level backward sparsity from forward-pass learnability

MECHANISM: During each forward pass, compute a free per-token "learnability" score from the existing logits (entropy × cross-entropy residual, no proxy model), then retain activations and run the backward pass only for the top-k% of tokens per microbatch, with the remaining tokens contributing forward context but no gradient. Because backward is ~2/3 of training FLOPs, a 50% token gate cuts step cost ~33% while *improving* gradient SNR by dropping both already-mastered tokens (near-zero gradient) and irreducibly noisy tokens (high-variance gradient), so loss-per-token-seen improves rather than degrades — the data-efficiency axis. Energy gains exceed FLOP gains because only gated tokens' activations are stored, shrinking HBM traffic and activation memory, which is where the joules and the recompute overhead actually live. The gate is a scalar threshold annealed on a running quantile, adding no parameters and no extra passes, so it composes with existing curricula and document-level filtering instead of competing with them.

TEST: Train a 150M-param decoder on 8B tokens at a fixed energy budget (measured via NVML joules) with gate ∈ {100% (baseline), 75%, 50%}, and check whether any gated run beats baseline simultaneously on validation loss vs. tokens-consumed *and* loss vs. joules — if gated runs only win on joules while losing on loss-per-token, the joint-frontier claim is false.

TITLE: Joule-Priced Token Routing: Optimizing Bits-of-Loss per Measured Watt

MECHANISM: Replace the usual per-step loss objective with a Lagrangian on *measured* energy: a lightweight router decides per-token how many transformer blocks (and which KV range) to spend, and its reward is loss-reduction-per-joule read live from on-device power counters (NVML/RAPL), not from a FLOP proxy. Because real joules are dominated by DRAM/HBM traffic rather than MACs, the router is pushed toward routing decisions that keep batches weight-stationary and cache-resident — a solution FLOP-based routing never finds. Data efficiency improves because the same mechanism concentrates depth on high-surprisal tokens (cheap tokens get shallow passes, so gradient signal per token is less diluted by already-learned n-gram structure); compute efficiency improves from the skipped blocks; energy efficiency improves beyond the FLOP saving because the price signal directly charges for memory movement. The key claim is that one price — joules — simultaneously induces token selection (data), depth sparsity (compute), and locality (energy), rather than trading them.

TEST: Train ~150M-param models for a fixed token budget on a single GPU with three routers — uniform depth, FLOP-priced, and joule-priced (NVML-in-the-loop) — and check whether the joule-priced run is strictly better on all three axes (val loss at matched tokens, at matched FLOPs, and at matched measured joules); losing on any one axis falsifies it.

TITLE: Just-in-time token assembly: forward-gated backward passes with shrinking buffers

MECHANISM: Standard training assumes every token materialized in a batch must receive a full backward pass, with data pre-shuffled and staged in bulk ahead of the optimizer. Invert this: the trainer *pulls* an oversized candidate batch, runs a low-precision forward pass only, then admits to the backward pass only the tokens whose per-token loss-gradient proxy exceeds a running threshold, repacking survivors into a dense sequence. Since backward+optimizer is ~2/3 of step FLOPs and nearly all of the optimizer-state HBM traffic, rejecting 40-60% of tokens cuts compute and joules super-linearly relative to the cheap fp8 forward overhead, while the admitted tokens are higher-signal so loss falls faster per token consumed. The candidate buffer multiplier is adapted downward as the admission rate stabilizes, so late training converges to near-zero overhead rather than paying a fixed selection tax.

TEST: Train a 160M model at matched *measured joules* (not tokens) on a single GPU with wall-power logging, comparing JIT gating against random batching — if validation loss at equal energy is not strictly better, and equal-token loss is not also better, the joint-frontier claim is dead.

TITLE: Learnability-gated token-sparse backpropagation with activation-stashing skipped

MECHANISM: During each forward pass, compute a per-token learnability score online (current model loss minus a running EMA of that token-type's loss, i.e. high-loss-but-still-decreasing tokens), then backpropagate only through the top-k fraction (~25%) of tokens, skipping activation stashing entirely for the rest. Data efficiency improves because the gradient budget concentrates on tokens that are still learnable rather than on already-mastered or irreducibly-noisy tokens, so loss-per-token-seen drops. Compute efficiency improves because backward is ~2/3 of training FLOPs and is now sublinear in sequence length, while the forward pass (needed anyway to score) is unchanged. Energy efficiency improves *super*-linearly with the FLOP saving because un-stashed activations never touch HBM — memory traffic, not arithmetic, dominates joules per training step, so joules/FLOP falls alongside FLOPs/token.

TEST: Train 150M-param models on 4B tokens with k=100% vs k=25% at matched wall-clock and matched tokens-seen, measuring validation loss plus wall-plug watt-hours; the idea dies if the k=25% run fails to beat baseline on at least two of {loss-at-fixed-tokens, loss-at-fixed-FLOPs, loss-at-fixed-Wh}.

TITLE: Bottom-Frozen Activation Replay: Reuse Cached Mid-Depth Features as Data

MECHANISM: Empirically the lowest third of a transformer's representations stabilize very early in pretraining; after that, re-running those layers on every token is redundant work. Once a per-layer drift metric falls below threshold, freeze layers 1..k and write their output activations for high-value sequences to disk as 4-bit quantized "feature shards" (with dequantization noise acting as augmentation), then train the upper 2/3 for several extra passes over the shard corpus interleaved with fresh tokens. This lifts data efficiency because each unique token yields multiple cheap upper-layer gradient steps at different noise/curriculum positions rather than one; it lifts compute efficiency because replay steps cost only (1-k/L) of forward+backward FLOPs; and it lifts energy efficiency superlinearly because frozen layers eliminate their optimizer-state and weight-gradient DRAM traffic entirely while shard reads are long sequential streams with far higher arithmetic intensity than tokenizer/embedding-bound fresh-data steps.

TEST: Train a 160M model on a 3B-token budget and compare, at matched wall-clock joules measured from the power rail, final validation loss against a standard run — if replay's loss-per-joule and loss-per-unique-token are not both strictly better, the idea fails.

TITLE: Nested Aperture Curriculum: growth-gated Matryoshka width-and-context scaling

MECHANISM: Train a single transformer whose width, attention span, and numeric precision are nested prefixes (Matryoshka-style), starting at a "blurred" configuration — low-rank embeddings, short local receptive field, low-precision accumulators — and expanding only when a measured saturation signal fires (residual-stream spectral energy escaping the active prefix, or plateau in marginal loss-per-token within the active subspace). Every stage is a complete, functional model, so expansion is a strict superset that reuses all prior weights with zero restart cost, and new capacity is initialized to be gradient-aligned with the residual the small model cannot explain. This helps data efficiency because coarse stages impose a strong low-frequency inductive bias that extracts broad distributional structure from few tokens, leaving later high-capacity stages to spend samples only on the genuinely high-frequency residual rather than relearning basics. It helps compute efficiency because most optimizer steps run at a fraction of full FLOPs, and energy efficiency independently because narrow, short-span, low-precision stages are memory-bandwidth-light — and joules are dominated by DRAM traffic, not FLOPs, so energy drops superlinearly relative to the FLOP saving.

TEST: Train ~150M-parameter models on ~3B tokens — fixed-width baseline vs. growth-gated nested run — and check whether the nested run Pareto-dominates on all three curves simultaneously (loss vs. tokens, loss vs. FLOPs, loss vs. wall-clock joules measured at the socket); failure on any single axis falsifies it.

TITLE: Learnability-gated sparse backpropagation using free early-layer exit scores

MECHANISM: A lightweight linear head attached to layer ~L/4 predicts each token's final-layer loss during the normal forward pass, so the score costs no extra passes. Tokens predicted to be already-mastered or irreducibly noisy are dropped from the backward graph only (loss is still computed forward), so with ~50% token masking the backward's 2/3 of FLOPs shrinks by half, cutting step cost ~33% and, more importantly, cutting stored activations and HBM read/write traffic — the dominant energy term — by a similar factor, since masked tokens need no saved intermediates. Data efficiency improves because the gradient budget concentrates on the high-learnability middle band rather than being diluted by the large fraction of trivially predictable tokens in web text, which is the same signal RHO-style selection exploits but obtained without a separate reference model or extra forward compute. Because the gate is internal and self-calibrating, the masking rate can anneal as the model's competence shifts, so all three axes move together rather than trading off.

TEST: Train 150M-parameter models on 6B tokens of FineWeb with and without the gate at matched wall-clock and matched measured joules (nvidia-smi integration), and check whether the gated run reaches equal-or-lower held-out loss at both equal tokens-seen and equal energy; failure on either comparison falsifies it.

TITLE: Bit-Activity Regularization: Switching Energy as an MDL Prior

MECHANISM: Add a differentiable penalty on the expected bit-transition/Hamming activity of the *actual low-precision datapath* — the quantized weight and activation words as they would stream through multipliers — computed via straight-through gradients on a bit decomposition, annealed like a KL term. Because dynamic energy in digital MAC arrays scales with switching activity, not nominal FLOPs, this directly cuts joules per step; the pressure also drives weights toward few-nonzero-bit (near power-of-two, shift-encodable) codes, so kernels can replace multiplies with shift-adds and skip zero bit-planes, cutting wall-clock compute. Crucially the same penalty is a genuine minimum-description-length prior over parameters (bit-activity ≈ code length), so it should *improve* sample efficiency rather than cost it — the usual quantization story runs backwards here, with the hardware-cheapness objective doing the regularizing work normally bought by more data. All three axes move together because one term simultaneously shortens the description, the arithmetic, and the switching.

TEST: Train a ~150M-param model on a fixed 5B-token budget with and without the bit-activity penalty and compare validation loss at matched tokens alongside a gate-level switching-activity energy estimate; if loss-vs-tokens is worse (no MDL gain), the joint-frontier claim is dead.

TITLE: Evaporating Data-Side Trails for Token-Level Depth and Sampling Routing

MECHANISM: Invert the assumption that the dataset is stateless and every token gets identical compute: attach a small persistent scalar "trail" value to each token position (and, via hashed n-gram/cluster keys, to unseen positions that share context), written for free from quantities the backward pass already computes (per-token loss, logit-margin change, gradient-norm proxy) and decayed multiplicatively each epoch so obsolete marks fade. At each step, trails gate two things at once: which sequences are drawn into the batch, and how many transformer layers each token traverses before early exit, so tokens the model has already mastered are learned-from cheaply while contested tokens get full depth. Because the trail generalizes through shared hash keys, a token never visited still inherits a compute estimate, avoiding the extra probe forward passes that make standard data-selection and mixture-of-depths methods compute-negative. Data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on still-informative tokens, compute and energy improve simultaneously because average layers-per-token and redundant re-reads both fall, and decay prevents the self-reinforcing collapse where the model only ever revisits a shrinking subset.

TEST: Train a 130M-parameter model on 2–4B tokens and check whether the trail-routed run beats a uniform-sampling, full-depth baseline on validation loss at *both* matched wall-clock FLOPs/joules *and* matched unique tokens seen; failure to dominate on both axes at once falsifies it.

TITLE: Learnability-gated selective backprop: cheap no-grad scoring, expensive gradients only where useful

MECHANISM: Each step, run a large superbatch through the model in inference mode (bf16, no activation stashing, flash-attention forward only) and score every sequence by *learnability* = current loss minus a per-sequence reference loss cached once from a small proxy model, so high-loss-but-noisy/unlearnable text is rejected along with already-mastered text. Only the top-k fraction (~25–40%) is re-run with gradients and backpropagated, so the step costs ≈ 1 cheap forward over N sequences + 3 units over 0.3N instead of 3N. Data efficiency improves because gradient updates concentrate on the learnable frontier (RHO-1-style gains) while — unlike token-level selection — the savings are realized *before* the backward pass rather than after. Energy improves superlinearly versus FLOPs because the scoring forward has no optimizer state traffic, no activation writes, and near-peak arithmetic intensity, so its joules-per-FLOP is roughly 2–3× better than a training step's; cached reference losses mean no second model is resident at train time.

TEST: Train a 150M-param model on 2B tokens of FineWeb-Edu at a *fixed measured-joules* budget (wall-plug or NVML-integrated) against a uniform-sampling baseline, and check whether selective-backprop reaches lower held-out loss at equal energy *and* equal unique-tokens-consumed — failing either equality kills it.

TITLE: Precomputed n-gram surprisal as static per-token compute and loss schedule

MECHANISM: Before training, make one cheap CPU pass over the corpus with a streaming suffix-array/n-gram model and store each token's count-based surprisal as a single byte alongside it. That static score then sets three things per token with zero runtime routing cost: how many transformer blocks the token traverses (low-surprisal tokens exit after a shallow prefix and are carried forward by a linear skip), how much its loss is weighted, and its activation precision. Because the allocation is known before the forward pass, the data loader sorts tokens into depth-homogeneous buckets so every kernel runs dense and fully packed — unlike learned mixture-of-depths routing, there is no load imbalance, no gather/scatter, and no router gradient. Data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on tokens carrying information a count model cannot already supply; compute efficiency improves because layer-token FLOPs drop ~30–50% at matched loss; energy efficiency improves superlinearly because static bucketing eliminates the DRAM traffic and pipeline bubbles that dominate joules in dynamic-depth schemes.

TEST: Train 150M-param models on 3B tokens — uniform-depth baseline vs. surprisal-scheduled — and check whether the scheduled run is strictly better on all three curves (loss vs. tokens, vs. FLOPs, vs. wall-plug joules measured by RAPL/NVML); a single axis regressing falsifies it.

TITLE: Surprisal-gated depth routing with redundant-token pruning and dense repacking

MECHANISM: A near-free streaming n-gram/hash predictor (updated online, <1% FLOPs) scores every token's residual novelty against what the model has already overlearned; tokens whose next-token distribution is already resolved by shallow features are exited after the first k transformer blocks, dropped from the loss, and — at the sequence level — removed from the replay stream so their budget is spent on genuinely novel text. Because exited token slots are compacted and the surviving deep-path tokens are contiguously repacked into full-width batches, the saved FLOPs convert into real wall-clock and joules rather than ragged, underutilized kernels. Data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on high-information tokens instead of habitual, low-entropy continuations; compute efficiency improves because average depth per token falls; energy efficiency improves superlinearly because dense repacking cuts HBM traffic and activation memory, which dominate joules-per-FLOP. The critical design constraint is that the gate must be model-derived and adaptive, so it retires patterns only after they are mastered rather than permanently starving rare-but-hard tokens.

TEST: Train a 160M model on a fixed 6B-token corpus with and without the gate on identical hardware, logging wall-clock and socket-level joules; the idea is falsified if gated runs fail to beat baseline validation loss at matched energy *and* matched tokens-seen simultaneously.

TITLE: Self-Referenced Learnability Gating of the Backward Pass

MECHANISM: Keep the full forward pass dense, but compute a per-token "learnability" score as current loss minus an exponential-moving-average of that token-type/context-bucket's historical loss, then run the backward pass only through the top-k% of tokens (gradients zeroed elsewhere, so activations for dropped tokens are freed immediately rather than stored). Unlike reference-model token selection (RHO-1), the baseline is the model's own cheap running statistic, so no second network is paid for. Data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on tokens that are neither already-memorized nor irreducibly noisy; compute efficiency improves because backward is ~2/3 of training FLOPs, so gating 50% of tokens removes ~33% of step FLOPs; energy efficiency improves super-linearly to the FLOP saving because dropped-token activation gradients never touch HBM, and activation-memory traffic — not arithmetic — dominates joules per step at long context.

TEST: Train a 160M-parameter decoder on 6B tokens with k=50% versus a dense baseline at three matched budgets (tokens, FLOPs, and measured wall-clock/joules via nvidia-smi integration) and check whether the gated run is Pareto-dominant on all three; any single-axis regression falsifies it.

TITLE: Precision Annealing as Learning-Rate Schedule: Arithmetic Noise as Optimizer Temperature

MECHANISM: Instead of decaying the learning rate, hold it fixed and anneal the *numerical precision* of forward/backward matmuls upward (e.g. ~3-bit weights/activations with stochastic rounding early, rising to 8-bit late), so that quantization noise — not the LR — supplies the SGD "temperature" that decays over training. This helps data efficiency because rounding noise is multiplicative in activation/weight magnitude and therefore anisotropic and roughly Fisher-aligned, a structurally better implicit regularizer than the isotropic noise an LR schedule scales, plausibly reaching a given loss in fewer tokens. It helps compute efficiency because low-bit tensor-core throughput is 2–8× higher exactly during the long early phase where full precision is provably wasted (gradient SNR ≪ 1 there). It helps energy independently of FLOP count because joules are dominated by bits moved and bit-width-quadratic multiplier cost, so the same step at 3 bits costs a small fraction of the energy of an 8-bit step — the three gains come from one knob rather than trading against each other.

TEST: Train a ~50M-parameter model on a fixed 2B-token budget comparing (a) cosine-LR at 8-bit versus (b) constant-LR with 3→8-bit annealing, and declare it falsified if (b) fails to dominate (a) simultaneously on loss-vs-tokens and loss-vs-modeled-joules (bit-width-weighted MAC + DRAM-traffic energy model).

TITLE: Shelf-Ordered Training: Hierarchical Document Codes Route Both Batches and Parameters

MECHANISM: Replace IID shuffling and monolithic dense weights with a single shared hierarchical address space: a cheap frozen encoder assigns every document a fixed-length coarse-to-fine code (e.g. 4 levels × 16 branches), and the FFN blocks become nested residual experts indexed by that code's prefixes, so a token's update touches the shared trunk plus only the ~4 branch modules on its path. Training then streams documents in code-sorted order rather than shuffled order, so consecutive steps reuse the same leaf experts. Data efficiency improves because topically coherent batches raise the effective gradient signal per token and confine destructive interference to a branch instead of smearing it across all parameters; compute efficiency improves because only a path-depth slice of the FFN parameters is active per token, unlike learned MoE routing this path is known before the forward pass, enabling static prefetch and no router/balancing overhead. Energy improves for a reason orthogonal to FLOPs: training joules are dominated by off-chip weight movement, and code-sorted streaming keeps the active branch resident in on-package memory across thousands of steps, collapsing HBM/DRAM traffic per token rather than merely trading it against arithmetic.

TEST: At ~150M params and a fixed 3B-token budget, train (a) dense shuffled, (b) dense code-sorted, (c) hierarchical-expert code-sorted, and check whether (c) simultaneously beats (a) on held-out loss, active-FLOPs/token, and measured joules/token (nvidia-smi integration plus DRAM-traffic counters) — if (c) only wins on FLOPs while losing loss to (a), or if its energy win vanishes once curriculum-induced forgetting forces replay, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Early-exit learnability gating: skip depth and backprop for settled tokens

MECHANISM: Insert a cheap linear probe at layer k (~1/3 depth) that predicts each token's remaining loss from its hidden state, trained online against the actual final-layer loss. Tokens predicted to be already-learned (low loss) or irreducibly noisy (high loss but high reference-model loss too) exit at layer k: they skip the remaining forward layers, store no activations, and contribute no gradient; surviving tokens are compacted into dense GEMMs so the ragged batch never degrades kernel utilization. This helps data efficiency because the gradient budget concentrates on the high-learnability band rather than being diluted by memorized boilerplate and noise; compute efficiency because ~40–60% of tokens traverse only a third of the network in both forward and backward passes; and energy efficiency super-linearly in the FLOP saving because dropped tokens also drop their activation stashes, cutting the HBM read/write traffic that dominates joules-per-FLOP on modern accelerators. The three axes are coupled rather than traded: the same signal that says "this token teaches nothing" is what authorizes skipping its compute and its memory traffic.

TEST: Train two 160M-param models on identical 4B-token streams — baseline vs. gated — and check whether the gated run reaches lower validation loss at matched tokens seen *and* lower loss at matched measured GPU-joules (nvidia-smi integration); failure on either axis falsifies the no-trade claim.

TITLE: Gradient Quadrature: Backprop on a Coreset, Extrapolate Gradients Forward-Only

MECHANISM: Instead of backpropagating every token, run all tokens forward-only and compute exact gradients for a small "anchor" subset chosen to span the batch's activation geometry; for non-anchor tokens, estimate their gradient contribution by projecting their final-layer activations onto the anchors' activation basis and reusing the anchors' already-materialized backward quantities (a Nyström-style quadrature over the batch in activation space, refreshed every step). Data efficiency improves because *every* token still influences the update through the quadrature weights rather than being discarded like in loss-based pruning. Compute efficiency improves because backward is ~2/3 of FLOPs and is now paid on only a fraction of tokens. Energy efficiency improves super-linearly relative to FLOPs because skipping backward also eliminates activation stashing/recomputation for those tokens, and forward-only inference-shaped passes have much higher arithmetic intensity and lower DRAM joules per FLOP than backward passes.

TEST: Train a 100M-param model on ~2B tokens with 25% anchor fraction and check whether it matches the full-backprop baseline's loss-vs-tokens curve while beating it on loss-vs-measured-joules; if it tracks the "anchors-only, non-anchors discarded" control instead, the quadrature term carries no signal and the idea is dead.

TITLE: Shortcut-Claimed Tokens: Let Cheap Predictors Exempt Themselves From Depth

MECHANISM: Standard training assumes every token deserves an identical full-depth forward and a gradient of equal standing; we invert this by making depth and gradient eligibility something a token must *earn*. A cheap early-exit head (layers 1–4 plus an n-gram/copy detector) may "claim" a token by declaring a confident prediction; claimed tokens skip the remaining layers and are excluded from the backward pass, while their saved FLOPs are reinvested into extra optimizer steps on the unclaimed residual, so the full network only ever sees tokens where the cheap route provably fails. To stop degenerate self-exemption, a small random audit fraction of claimed tokens is run at full depth; any head whose claims the deep model disagrees with pays a large penalty and its confidence threshold tightens, making over-claiming strictly unprofitable. This should move all three axes together rather than trade them: compute and energy drop because the majority of highly predictable tokens (whitespace, boilerplate, copied spans) never touch the deep stack or the backward graph, and data efficiency rises because the fixed update budget is concentrated on high-surprise tokens that carry nearly all the learning signal per token consumed.

TEST: Train a ~150M-parameter model on ~4B tokens against a dense baseline and check whether it strictly dominates on *both* loss-versus-FLOPs and loss-versus-tokens-seen curves simultaneously — matching on one while losing the other falsifies the joint-frontier claim.

TITLE: Learnability-gated token routing: skip depth on low-value tokens

MECHANISM: During training, a cheap online score computed from the first k transformer layers (current-model entropy minus a running reference-model estimate, i.e. a reducible-loss proxy) gates each token at a mid-network exit point; tokens that are already mastered or irreducibly noisy exit early and are dropped from the loss, while high-learnability tokens traverse the full depth and receive full gradients. Unlike offline data filtering, the gate adapts as the model learns, so the same corpus keeps yielding useful signal — improving data efficiency. Because skipped tokens never execute the upper layers in forward or backward, per-step FLOPs, activation memory traffic, and optimizer-relevant work all fall, giving compute efficiency rather than paying for selection. Energy follows compute plus the reduced HBM traffic from shorter sequences in the upper stack, and the gate itself is free because it reuses logits from an existing intermediate layer with a tied readout head.

TEST: Train 160M-parameter models on 4B tokens of FineWeb-Edu with gate keep-rates {1.0, 0.5, 0.25} and check whether the gated runs dominate the baseline on validation loss plotted against measured GPU joules — if no keep-rate beats the baseline curve at matched energy, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Semantically Coherent Batching for Delta-Compressed, Low-Switching Training

MECHANISM: Instead of i.i.d. shuffling, each microbatch is assembled from nearest neighbors in a cheap frozen embedding space (a "locality-ordered" stream that is globally shuffled at the cluster level, so no curriculum drift), and all intra-step tensor traffic — KV cache, MLP intermediates, activation checkpoints, gradient all-reduce payloads — is stored and moved as deltas against the batch's centroid activation rather than as absolute values. Because near-duplicate inputs produce near-identical activations, those deltas are low-entropy and low-magnitude, which cuts HBM/interconnect bytes (the dominant energy term, not FLOPs) and cuts datapath bit-flips in the multipliers, giving real joules-per-step savings and wall-clock savings from bandwidth relief. Data efficiency should rise rather than fall because a batch of semantic near-neighbors is implicitly a hard-negative set: the gradient is dominated by the fine distinctions the model actually confuses, so each token carries more information per unit compute than a batch of mutually irrelevant documents. The three axes are coupled by one property — intra-batch redundancy — which simultaneously makes activations compressible and makes the loss surface locally contrastive, so tightening it helps all three instead of trading among them.

TEST: Train two 100M-param models to the same token budget, one with shuffled batches and one with neighbor-clustered batches, and check whether the clustered run both matches/beats validation loss and shows materially lower measured activation-delta entropy and bit-flip counts; failure on either half falsifies it.

TITLE: Backward-sparse token sampling with free online gradient-norm control variates

MECHANISM: Every token still gets a full forward pass (context is never discarded), but the backward pass is run through only a fraction k of sequence positions at the LM head and upper blocks, with the rest's position-gradients zeroed and the survivors importance-reweighted so the update stays unbiased. Naive random subsampling fails because per-token gradient magnitude is extremely heavy-tailed, so the estimator's variance eats the FLOP savings — the fix is a nearly-free control variate: a single linear probe on the already-computed final hidden state, trained online to predict per-token gradient norm, used as the sampling proposal plus a baseline correction term. This helps data efficiency (update mass concentrates on high-information tokens rather than the ~60% of tokens that are already near-deterministic), compute efficiency (backward is ~2/3 of FLOPs and the large-vocab output projection is skipped for unsampled positions), and energy efficiency (activation gradients and optimizer traffic for skipped positions never leave SRAM, cutting HBM bandwidth, which dominates joules per step more than FLOPs do). The three gains compound rather than trade because nothing is thrown away at acquisition time — only the redundant half of the *gradient* measurement is skipped, and the probe restores the discarded structure instead of assuming it is zero.

TEST: Train a 160M-parameter model on 4B tokens at k=0.5 versus a full-backward baseline matched on measured wall-clock joules (RAPL/nvidia-smi integration), and check whether validation loss at equal energy is strictly lower and at equal tokens is no worse — if either fails, or if ablating the control variate to uniform sampling closes the gap, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Learnability-gated sparse backward passes with recycled forward statistics

MECHANISM: During the standard forward pass we already compute a per-token loss; define a learnability score as (current loss − EMA of that token's earlier loss under the same model) and keep only the top-k% of tokens (k≈30–40) as "gradient-carrying." For the backward pass, unselected positions still serve as keys/values in attention (so context is preserved and no accuracy is lost from truncation), but we skip their unembedding/LM-head gradient and their MLP-block backward, which is where most of the per-token backward FLOPs and memory traffic live. This should improve data efficiency because gradient budget is concentrated on tokens that are neither already-learned nor noise-saturated (the same mechanism that makes RHO-style token selection beat uniform loss), compute efficiency because backward is ~2× forward cost and we remove a large structured fraction of it, and energy efficiency super-linearly because the skipped work is dominated by HBM traffic for activations and the large vocab logit matrix rather than by FLOPs. The key claim is that selection quality and cost reduction come from the *same* signal, so there is no scoring overhead (no reference model, no extra forward) and no three-way trade.

TEST: Train 150M-param models on 6B tokens of FineWeb-Edu — baseline vs. this method — and compare validation loss at matched measured wall-clock *and* matched GPU joules (nvidia-smi integration); if the method fails to strictly dominate the baseline on both matched-energy and matched-token curves, it is falsified.

TITLE: Gradient-Coherent Batch Scheduling for Larger Steps and Compressible Optimizer State

MECHANISM: Maintain a near-free per-example gradient sketch (a random projection of the last-layer/output-embedding gradient, computable from the forward pass) and use it to build each batch from examples whose sketches are mutually aligned, while a Latin-square schedule over sketch clusters keeps the epoch-level sample distribution unbiased. Coherent batches cancel less signal internally, so the same token budget yields a larger useful update — permitting a higher stable learning rate and fewer optimizer steps (compute), and the sketch simultaneously exposes near-duplicate gradient directions that can be dropped without loss of information (data). Because the momentum direction then drifts slowly and predictably between steps, the optimizer state becomes a low-entropy residual against a one-step linear predictor and can be stored at ~4 bits, cutting the DRAM/HBM traffic that dominates joules-per-step (energy). The three gains share one cause — induced gradient coherence — rather than trading against each other.

TEST: Train a 100M-param model on ~2B tokens with i.i.d. versus sketch-clustered batching and check whether clustering raises the maximum stable learning rate and lowers the entropy of momentum-prediction residuals; if neither moves, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Reconciliation-Gated Training: Balanced Loss Ledgers Select Tokens and Backward Passes

MECHANISM: Every microbatch token gets two paired entries: a *predicted* loss (from a frozen EMA/draft copy plus a first-order extrapolation of the last update's effect on that token) and the *realized* loss from the current forward pass; the signed residual between them is the token's unexplained learning signal. Only tokens whose ledgers fail to balance beyond a running tolerance are admitted to the backward pass and optimizer update, so ~60–80% of tokens cost a forward pass only — cutting FLOPs, activation-memory traffic, and therefore joules per token, while concentrating gradient capacity on genuinely novel tokens (data efficiency). Crucially, skipped tokens are not discarded but booked as outstanding liabilities against their data shard; a periodic "trial balance" re-audits shards with large accumulated unbalanced mass, which is what prevents the silent distribution drift and late-training quality collapse that sinks ordinary loss-thresholded data selection, so the three axes improve together instead of trading off. The tolerance is set so the total booked residual mass per step stays constant, making the gate self-calibrating across training phases without a tuned schedule.

TEST: Train a 160M-parameter model on 8B tokens with and without the gate, logging tokens consumed, total FLOPs, and wall-plug joules — the idea is falsified if the gated run fails to match baseline validation loss while strictly reducing all three, or if removing the liability/re-audit ledger changes nothing (showing the gain is plain loss-thresholding).

TITLE: Early-Exit Token Routing with Reinvested Compute Budget

MECHANISM: After a shallow prefix (e.g., first 4 of 24 layers), a cheap linear scorer predicts each token's remaining learnable signal (proxy: prefix-head cross-entropy plus its EMA-normalized drop since the token's last visit); low-signal positions exit, skipping the deep stack in both forward and backward, while their prefix-head loss still supervises them. The saved FLOPs are not banked as speedup but reinvested by raising tokens-per-step at fixed wall-clock, so the deep stack's gradient budget is concentrated almost entirely on high-signal tokens. This should improve data efficiency (more informative gradient per token seen), compute efficiency (fewer FLOPs per unit loss reduction, since easy-token deep activations are near-redundant), and energy efficiency simultaneously, because energy tracks FLOPs *and* activation memory traffic — skipped tokens shrink the stored activation set superlinearly with depth. The joint gain is possible rather than a trade because the mechanism removes near-zero-gradient work instead of reallocating useful work between axes.

TEST: Train a 160M-param model to a fixed validation-loss target on a fixed corpus with and without the router, logging tokens consumed, total FLOPs, and wall-plug joules (RAPL/NVML integration) — the idea is falsified if the router fails to strictly dominate the baseline on all three at that target, or if exit decisions collapse to a depth-uniform/random pattern.

TITLE: N-gram residual logits with prior-restricted softmax for transformer LMs

MECHANISM: Build a static suffix-automaton/count-based n-gram predictor over the training corpus and, at every position, add its log-probabilities as a fixed (non-learned) additive prior to the model's logits, so the transformer is trained only on the *residual* the lookup table cannot explain. Because the prior already concentrates mass, the full vocabulary projection is replaced by a softmax over the union of the prior's top-K candidates plus sampled negatives with an importance correction, shrinking the output matmul — typically 20–40% of small-model FLOPs and a large share of DRAM traffic — to a fraction of its cost. Data efficiency improves because gradient signal and capacity are no longer spent relearning exactly-known copy/collocation statistics; compute efficiency improves from the truncated head and from the residual target being lower-entropy and faster-fitting; energy efficiency improves superlinearly because a table lookup costs picojoules while the eliminated vocab matmul costs both arithmetic and high-bandwidth weight reads.

TEST: Train a 160M-parameter model for 2B tokens with and without the n-gram prior + restricted head on identical hardware, and check whether held-out bits-per-byte is strictly lower at equal measured joules *and* at equal tokens seen — if either equality fails, the joint-frontier claim is falsified.

TITLE: Affinity-Gated Micro-Expert Repertoires with Mutation, Memory, and Negative Selection

MECHANISM: Replace the upper MLP stack with a large repertoire of very small, mostly-frozen low-rank expert modules; the first few shared layers emit a cheap signature per token-span that is matched against expert key vectors, and only the top-k highest-affinity experts are activated *and* receive gradients, so both forward and backward cost scale with k, not repertoire size. Experts that repeatedly win and reduce loss are duplicated with perturbed initialization (mutate-and-select) so capacity is allocated only where the data distribution actually exerts pressure, while experts with persistently negative marginal contribution are pruned and their slots recycled — capacity growth is demand-driven rather than pre-provisioned. A consolidation memory stores signatures of spans already handled at near-zero residual loss; spans matching memory above threshold are forwarded through the shared trunk plus one memory-summoned expert and skipped for the backward pass entirely. Data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on unmastered, high-information spans; compute efficiency improves because activated and differentiated parameters are a small fraction of total; energy efficiency improves on top of FLOP savings because frozen experts need no optimizer state traffic and skipped spans avoid the backward pass, cutting the memory-bandwidth work that dominates joules per token.

TEST: Train a ~120M-active-parameter model on 3B tokens against a dense baseline matched on measured wall-clock joules (RAPL/NVML), and check whether it reaches lower validation loss at equal energy *and* equal tokens consumed — if either axis is merely traded off, the claim fails.

TITLE: FP8 No-Grad Triage: Score Every Batch, Backprop the Learnable Quarter

MECHANISM: Each step, run a grad-free FP8 forward over a 4x-oversampled microbatch (no activation storage, ~1/6 the energy of a full fwd+bwd step) and score every sequence by *learnability* = current loss minus an EMA-of-self reference loss, which isolates examples that are neither already-mastered nor irreducibly noisy. Only the top-25% of sequences are re-run in BF16 with activations and backprop, so the optimizer sees higher-gradient-norm, lower-redundancy batches at ~0.9x the FLOPs of a standard step on 1x data. Data efficiency improves because mastered and noisy tokens are never granted gradient updates; compute efficiency improves because the discarded 75% never pay the 2x backward or the activation-memory cost; energy efficiency improves super-linearly because the dominant DRAM/HBM traffic term (activation read/write, optimizer-state touches per useful update) is what gets eliminated, and the triage pass is compute-dense FP8 at near-peak arithmetic intensity. The EMA-of-self reference removes the need for a separately trained proxy scorer, which is where prior learnability-based selection methods lost their compute savings.

TEST: Train 150M-param models for a fixed *measured joules* budget (wall-clock power logging via NVML) on FineWeb-Edu and check whether triage beats the standard-training baseline on held-out loss at equal energy, equal wall-clock, *and* equal unique tokens consumed simultaneously — failure on any one of the three axes falsifies it.

TITLE: Pointer-Elided Pretraining: Redundant Spans Replaced by Cached-KV Copy Tokens

MECHANISM: Before training, run a cheap suffix-automaton/MinHash pass that finds spans in each document that are verbatim or near-verbatim recurrences of spans already committed to a small frozen "cache corpus"; replace each such span in the training stream with a single pointer token whose embedding is a pooled vector, and let the model attend to the cached span's precomputed (once, offline, in low precision) KV entries through a dedicated retrieval-attention head. The model is trained to emit the pointer token where the span is fully predictable-by-copy and to emit literal text otherwise, so gradient signal concentrates on genuinely novel content instead of being spent re-deriving boilerplate, license text, templated markup, and quote chains that dominate web corpora. Data efficiency improves because each retained token carries higher marginal information per optimizer step; compute efficiency improves because effective sequence length drops superlinearly under quadratic attention while the cached KV is amortized across every document that points at it; energy efficiency improves for a reason distinct from FLOPs — elided spans never enter HBM as activations or optimizer traffic, and DRAM movement, not arithmetic, is the dominant joule cost in pretraining. Crucially none of the three is traded for another, because the same eliminated bytes are simultaneously the low-information, high-FLOP, high-memory-traffic bytes.

TEST: Pretrain a 150M-parameter model on a fixed 10B-token web slice with and without pointer elision, matched on measured wall-clock joules rather than tokens or steps, and check whether the elided run has lower held-out loss on a redundancy-stripped evaluation set — if it does not beat baseline at equal energy, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Early-Bound Multiplicative Gating: One Cheap Plan Controls Whole-Depth Compute

MECHANISM: Energy in training is dominated by moving bytes, not multiplying them, so the win comes from never fetching weights you will not use — which requires knowing that *before* the layer runs. After the embedding plus one shallow block, a tiny controller (<0.5% of FLOPs) emits, for each token, a full-depth plan: which contiguous channel-groups of every FFN/attention block are active, plus a per-group multiplicative scale applied to the *existing* weights. Because the plan is bound early and groups are memory-contiguous, inactive weights are never read from HBM (energy), the FLOPs are genuinely skipped with prefetch hiding the latency (compute), and the multiplicative scaling lets one parameter set express combinatorially many effective functions, so specialization emerges without adding parameters (data efficiency). The controller is also trained with a scalar budget penalty, so it spontaneously allocates more depth-active capacity to high-loss tokens — a learned curriculum rather than a uniform one, which is exactly why sample efficiency should rise rather than merely hold.

TEST: Train a ~160M-parameter model on ~6B tokens against a dense baseline and a standard per-layer top-k MoE/MoD baseline, plot loss against (tokens, FLOPs, measured joules from on-device power counters) simultaneously, and reject the idea if it fails to strictly dominate the dense baseline on all three curves — especially if measured joules fail to drop proportionally to the skipped FLOPs, which would show the memory-traffic argument is wrong.

TITLE: Reducibility-gated token backprop via free early-exit disagreement signal

MECHANISM: Attach a lightweight linear exit head to an intermediate layer (~L/4) trained jointly; during each forward pass its prediction disagreement with the full model's output gives a free per-token "reducibility" score with zero extra forward FLOPs. Only the top-k% highest-disagreement tokens per batch are kept in the backward pass — MLP and output-head backward gathers just those token rows (the dominant FLOP term), while attention backward runs dense on the packed sequence. This helps data efficiency because gradient signal concentrates on tokens the model has not yet compressed rather than on already-memorized boilerplate; compute efficiency because backward is ~2/3 of training FLOPs and is now sublinear in sequence tokens; and energy efficiency because the gathered token rows form fixed-shape dense GEMMs (k is constant per batch), keeping tensor-core utilization high so joules/FLOP does not regress the way it does with unstructured sparsity or variable-shape routing.

TEST: Train 160M-param models on 10B tokens with k=40% vs. a dense baseline at matched wall-clock and matched measured joules (nvidia-smi sampling), and check whether held-out loss is strictly lower on both budgets — if gated loss is worse at equal energy, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Forward-only gradient sketches to skip redundant backward passes

MECHANISM: During each microbatch's forward pass, compute a near-free rank-1 proxy for its update direction — the output-layer error vector (p − y) outer-producted with the final hidden state, compressed by a fixed random projection into a ~256-dim signature — and compare it against a streaming sketch of directions already applied in the recent optimizer window. Microbatches whose signature is well-explained by the recent span are dropped before backprop and their tokens returned to the pool, so redundancy is measured in *gradient space* rather than text space, catching semantic duplicates and already-mastered content that n-gram dedup and loss-thresholding both miss. Data efficiency improves because the token budget is spent on genuinely novel update directions; compute efficiency improves because the skipped backward is ~2/3 of step FLOPs while the decision costs <0.1%; energy efficiency improves superlinearly because the backward pass dominates HBM traffic (activation reads, gradient and optimizer-state writes), and joules per token are traffic-bound, not FLOP-bound. Crucially the three gains are coupled rather than traded: the same skip event removes a token-slot's waste, its FLOPs, and its bytes moved.

TEST: Train a 150M-param model on 4B tokens and check whether sketch-based skipping at a 30% skip rate beats both no-skip and random-skip-at-matched-rate on loss-vs-tokens *and* loss-vs-FLOPs simultaneously — if it only wins on one axis, or ties random skipping, the gradient-space redundancy signal is worthless.

TITLE: Pull-Based Token Provisioning: Depth-Gated Just-In-Time Gradient Allocation

MECHANISM: Standard training pre-commits every token in a fixed batch to a full-depth forward and backward pass, stockpiling gradient signal for positions the model has already mastered. Instead, run only the first k of L layers on an oversized candidate batch, then use a tiny head on those shared shallow activations (plus the previous step's cached logits, already paid for) to score each position's expected learning value; only the top-p fraction of positions is carried through the remaining L−k layers and backward, with the deep stack's sequence dimension compacted just-in-time so microbatches fill the accelerator with no padding. Data efficiency improves because the fixed gradient budget is spent on high-surprisal, non-redundant positions rather than uniformly across a corpus that is mostly already-learned text; compute efficiency improves because cost per updated token falls to roughly k/L + p(1−k/L) of dense training; energy efficiency improves super-linearly with the FLOP saving because dropped positions never allocate deep-layer activations or KV state, cutting the HBM traffic and optimizer-state churn that dominate joules per token. The three axes move together rather than trading off because the selector consumes signal the forward pass already produces, so better targeting is not purchased with extra computation.

TEST: Train a ~120M-parameter model on a fixed 4B-token stream against a dense baseline and plot validation loss simultaneously against unique tokens consumed, total training FLOPs, and measured wall-clock joules — the idea is falsified if the gated run fails to dominate the baseline on all three curves at once (e.g., it matches loss-per-FLOP but needs more unique tokens, or saves FLOPs without saving measured energy).
