TITLE: Learnability-gated token masking with fused sparse backward passes

MECHANISM: A frozen ~10M-parameter reference model scores every token's loss online; positions where the trainee's loss is already within ε of the reference-implied entropy floor (or hopelessly above it) are dropped from the backward pass only, while the forward pass runs dense so context is never corrupted. The retained positions are compacted into variable-length batches by a fused gather/scatter kernel, so the backward GEMMs shrink proportionally instead of degenerating into masked dense work. Data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on tokens at the learnable frontier rather than on memorized boilerplate; compute efficiency improves because the backward is ~2/3 of training FLOPs and a 50% keep-rate removes ~33% of them at equal token exposure; energy efficiency improves super-linearly because dropped positions also eliminate their activation-gradient HBM traffic, and joules/FLOP is dominated by memory movement, not arithmetic. The three axes co-move because the same mask simultaneously removes low-information samples, low-value FLOPs, and the bytes those FLOPs would have moved.

TEST: Train two 150M-parameter models on identical 5B-token streams — dense baseline vs. 50%-keep gated backward — and check whether the gated run reaches equal or lower held-out loss at strictly lower wall-clock and lower measured device joules (NVML integration); failure of any one of the three inequalities falsifies it.

TITLE: Suffix-array prior as free teacher, router, and softmax sparsifier

MECHANISM: Build a streaming suffix-array/hash n-gram predictor over the training corpus (cost: ~1% of a single epoch, no gradients), and use its per-token distribution three ways simultaneously. (1) The model only learns the *residual* logits over the n-gram's top-K candidates plus a bucketed tail, so the output projection reads K×d instead of V×d weights — cutting the softmax/embedding FLOPs and, more importantly, the DRAM traffic that dominates joules at small-to-mid scale. (2) The n-gram's surprisal gates transformer depth per token: copy-like, locally-determined tokens exit after a few blocks with stop-gradient, while high-surprisal tokens get full depth and full backward. (3) Because gradient budget concentrates on tokens the corpus statistics cannot already explain, each token contributes more novel signal, so data efficiency improves rather than being traded away. The key claim is that all three axes share one bottleneck — spending capacity and memory bandwidth on locally-predictable tokens — so removing it moves them together.

TEST: Train a 100M-param model on 3B tokens against a matched baseline at *equal measured joules* (not equal steps) and check whether validation loss on held-out, low-n-gram-overlap text is lower; if the residual parameterization's candidate-set recall floors the loss above baseline, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Pull-Based Token Provisioning: Early-Exit Rejection Cascades with Demand-Sized Batches

MECHANISM: Instead of pushing fixed-size batches of pre-staged tokens through the full network, the trainer *pulls* only as much data as the current gradient signal demands: a shared prefix of the first k layers runs on a candidate stream and emits a cheap per-sequence utility estimate (predicted loss minus a running reference), and only sequences above a demand threshold are admitted to the remaining layers and the backward pass, while the rest are dropped after the truncated forward with no activation storage. The admission threshold and the accumulation depth are set online by the gradient noise scale, so the optimizer accumulates exactly until the batch's signal-to-noise crosses a target — no oversized batches held "in stock" against worst-case variance. Data efficiency improves because each admitted sequence is selected for current marginal utility rather than i.i.d. sampling; compute efficiency improves because rejected sequences cost only k/L of a forward and zero backward; energy efficiency improves on a third, partly independent axis because small demand-driven lots keep activations resident in SRAM and cut HBM traffic and idle memory-bound stalls, which dominate joules per FLOP. Crucially the shared prefix is the real model's own early layers, so the screening compute is not wasted overhead but reused work for admitted samples.

TEST: Train a ~300M-parameter model to a fixed validation loss on a single GPU with a power meter, comparing standard fixed-batch training against the pull-based variant, and check whether tokens consumed, total FLOPs, *and* measured wall-clock joules all drop simultaneously — any one of the three failing to improve falsifies it.

TITLE: FP8 Screen-Once Training: Reuse Screening Forward for Selective Backprop

MECHANISM: Each step, run a single FP8 forward pass over an oversampled candidate batch (e.g. 3x the target sequences) and score each sequence by a learnability signal computable from that same pass (current loss minus an EMA-of-own-predictions reference, which rejects both already-learned and unlearnable/noisy text). Instead of discarding and recomputing, retain the FP8 activations for the top-third scoring sequences and run backward directly on them, so the screening pass *is* the training forward pass — no duplicated compute. Data efficiency improves because gradients are spent only on sequences with high remaining learning signal; compute efficiency improves because screening costs ~0.5x a BF16 forward in FP8 and the skipped two-thirds never incur the 2x-forward backward cost (~2.5F vs 3F per effective sequence, before any data-quality gain); energy efficiency improves super-linearly with the FLOP reduction because FP8 halves HBM traffic and tensor-core joules/FLOP, and dropped sequences never touch optimizer-state memory bandwidth.

TEST: Train 150M-param models on identical token streams for a fixed *measured wall-clock and joule budget* (GPU power logged via NVML) against a uniform-sampling BF16 baseline, and check whether validation loss is strictly better on all three budget axes — data, FLOPs, and joules — simultaneously.

TITLE: Zero-FLOP suffix-automaton patching: corpus statistics as a free tokenizer

MECHANISM: Replace fixed BPE tokenization with dynamic byte-patching whose boundaries are set by an online suffix automaton built on CPU from the training stream itself, splitting only where the automaton's next-byte distribution is high-entropy and merging long, already-memorized spans into single patches. Unlike entropy-model patching (BLT), the segmenter costs zero GPU FLOPs and *improves as training proceeds*, so mean sequence length shrinks monotonically and compute-per-document falls over the run rather than staying fixed. Data efficiency improves because the transformer's gradient budget is spent on genuinely unpredictable residual structure instead of re-deriving copyable n-gram surface statistics; compute and energy improve because the same effect arrives as shorter sequences (fewer attention and MLP FLOPs and less HBM traffic per document), not as extra auxiliary-model passes. The three axes move together because one free statistical signal simultaneously selects *what* to model and *how much* activation to allocate to it.

TEST: Train a ~150M-param model to a fixed GPU-hour (not token) budget on 10B bytes with automaton patching versus BPE and versus BLT-style neural-entropy patching, and check whether validation bits-per-byte at equal measured wall-clock energy is at least as good while mean patch length grows over training — if BPE matches or beats it at equal joules, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Free-Riding Value Heads That Gate the Backward Pass

MECHANISM: Standard training assumes every token that enters the forward pass has earned a full backward pass, and that any data-selection module must pay for its own separate forward compute. Invert both: attach a ~1M-parameter linear "appraiser" head to a mid-layer of the host model that reads activations already computed by the host's forward pass (so its inference cost is ~0.1% overhead) and predicts each span's marginal loss reduction; the host then runs the backward pass only on the top-k fraction of spans per microbatch, with the rest contributing forward-only signal that trains the appraiser via its realized-vs-predicted loss delta. Because backward is ~2/3 of training FLOPs, dropping 40% of spans from it cuts compute and joules near-proportionally, while the appraiser's learned ranking means the surviving gradient budget lands on high-information spans, so tokens-to-target-loss also falls — the two modules pay each other in currencies neither spends extra compute to produce. A stress guard resamples a random 5% of skipped spans each step and reverts the gate toward uniform if appraiser calibration degrades, preventing the collapse mode where the gate starves the host of distributional coverage.

TEST: Train a 160M-parameter model on 4B tokens of FineWeb-Edu against an identical baseline at matched measured joules (via NVML) and matched wall-clock, and check whether gated training reaches strictly lower validation loss and lower tokens-consumed-to-equal-loss; if it only matches the baseline on any one of the three, the joint-frontier claim is dead.

TITLE: Learnability-gated token depth: early-exit scoring concentrates gradients and FLOPs

MECHANISM: Insert a tiny auxiliary loss-prediction head at ~25% depth that, from the already-computed intermediate activations, predicts each token's current cross-entropy and its EMA over recent epochs-equivalents; tokens whose predicted loss is either already near-zero (learned) or persistently high-entropy-irreducible (noise/unlearnable) exit the stack immediately and receive no further forward compute, no stored activations, and no gradient. The remaining high-learnability tokens traverse full depth and drive the backward pass, so the optimizer's signal is concentrated on the tokens where loss is actually moving — a data-efficiency gain that is the same mechanism as the compute saving rather than a trade against it. Because 75% of the layers run at the keep-rate in both forward and backward, FLOPs fall roughly proportionally, and dropped tokens also stop being written to activation memory, cutting HBM traffic which dominates joules-per-FLOP on modern accelerators. The gate is learned online and costs one linear head, so there is no separate proxy-model or offline-scoring pass to amortize, which is where prior data-selection methods lose their compute advantage.

TEST: Train a ~150M-parameter model on 4B tokens with keep-rate 0.5 versus a dense baseline on one GPU with a wall-plug power meter, and check whether validation loss is better at matched joules *and* at matched tokens seen; if either comparison fails to beat dense, the joint-frontier claim is falsified.

TITLE: Precision-Matched Data Pruning: arithmetic noise floor as the sample selector

MECHANISM: Represent every weight and activation as an ordered sum of bit-planes and train with only the top-k planes active, where k grows per-layer on a schedule driven by a measured signal-to-quantization-noise ratio. The key coupling: the current arithmetic noise floor is also used as the data filter — any token whose per-token gradient contribution falls below the noise floor of the active datapath is dropped from the backward pass (and its microbatch slot refilled), since spending energy on it is provably below the representable resolution. This makes one scalar simultaneously control multiply-accumulate energy (which scales roughly quadratically in mantissa width and linearly in DRAM bytes moved), FLOPs skipped, and tokens consumed, so the three axes move together instead of trading off; the low-precision early phase additionally acts as a structure-first regularizer that forces high-mass linguistic regularities to be learned before idiosyncratic detail. Unlike standard mixed precision (fixed schedule, all data) or loss-based pruning (extra forward passes), the selection signal is already computed by the quantizer for free.

TEST: Train ~100M-param models on a fixed token stream at matched joules (measured via RAPL/nvidia-smi), comparing coupled bit-plane+noise-floor pruning against (a) fixed bf16 with random pruning and (b) fixed bf16 with loss-thresholded pruning — if the coupled scheme does not Pareto-dominate on tokens-seen, FLOPs, and joules to a target validation loss, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Budgeted gradient exemptions: learned context-only spans with no-backward tax

MECHANISM: Standard pretraining assumes every token in the corpus is owed a gradient; here the model may legally opt out. A tiny online predictor (a linear probe on layer-k activations, trained to forecast per-span reducible loss = current loss minus an EMA of an irreducible-noise floor) marks a fixed budget of token spans as "exempt": they are still fed forward as context, but are wrapped in stop-gradient and excluded from the loss, so their activations are never stored, never recomputed, and never backpropagated through. A hard global exemption quota (e.g. 40%) prevents the degenerate solution of exempting everything easy or everything hard, forcing the probe to spend its allowance only where the gradient is mostly label noise, boilerplate, or already-memorized text. Data efficiency improves because the retained gradient signal has higher SNR per token consumed; compute and energy improve simultaneously because backward+recompute is ~2/3 of training FLOPs and is now sparse in the sequence dimension, with proportional activation-memory and HBM-traffic savings rather than a quality-for-speed trade.

TEST: Train 150M-param models on 4B tokens matched on wall-clock energy (measured joules), comparing uniform-loss baseline against 40%-exempt budgeted training, and check whether exempt-training reaches equal or lower validation loss at equal joules *and* equal tokens — if it wins on only one of the two axes, the joint-frontier claim is false.

TITLE: FP8 prefix scoring gates full backward passes on learnable tokens

MECHANISM: Each step draws an oversampled candidate batch and scores it with an FP8, prefix-only (first ~256 tokens) forward pass plus a frozen early-exit head, yielding a per-sequence "excess loss" (current model loss minus a cached reference-model loss) at roughly 5–10% of a full training step's cost. Only the top-k highest-excess-loss sequences receive the full BF16 forward+backward, so the expensive 2/3-of-FLOPs backward is spent exclusively on tokens that are neither already-learned nor unlearnable noise. Data efficiency improves because gradient signal per consumed token rises; compute efficiency improves because the selection overhead is far smaller than the FLOPs saved by skipping low-value backwards; energy efficiency improves super-linearly on top of that because the added work runs in FP8 (≈2–4× better joules/FLOP and lower memory-bandwidth energy) while the removed work was BF16 with full activation traffic. The key claim is that prefix-level, low-precision scores correlate well enough with full-sequence excess loss (Spearman ρ high) that the cheap proxy loses little selection quality.

TEST: Train a 200M-param model on a fixed corpus and compare validation loss against a uniform-sampling baseline at matched wall-clock, matched total FLOPs, and matched measured joules (RAPL/NVML), falsifying the idea if it fails to win on all three simultaneously — with a 1-GPU-hour pre-check that prefix FP8 excess-loss scores have Spearman ρ > 0.7 against full-sequence BF16 scores.

TITLE: Boosting Transformers on a Hashed N-gram Prior with Gradient-Gated Token Skipping

MECHANISM: Freeze a compact hashed n-gram/count model as an always-on additive logit prior, and train the transformer only to predict the *residual* of that prior rather than the full next-token distribution. Because a large fraction of natural-language tokens are already near-deterministic under local statistics, the residual target has near-zero gradient on those tokens, which lets a cheap online gate (residual cross-entropy under a threshold, computed from the prior alone *before* the forward pass) drop them from the backward pass and from deeper layers entirely. Data efficiency improves because every parameter update carries only information the cheap prior cannot express, so gradient noise from high-frequency filler tokens stops diluting the signal; compute efficiency improves because skipped tokens cost no backward FLOPs and truncated depth; energy efficiency improves *super-linearly* relative to compute because skipped tokens need no stored activations, cutting the DRAM traffic that dominates joules-per-FLOP, while the n-gram table is a sparse read from a few MB rather than a dense matmul. The key asymmetry is that the gate is computed from a model that costs ~0 FLOPs, so the selection overhead does not eat the savings, unlike loss-based or model-confidence-based token dropping.

TEST: Train a 160M-param model on 4B tokens with and without the prior+gate at *matched wall-clock energy* (measured via RAPL/nvidia-smi integration) and check whether the residual-trained run reaches lower held-out full-distribution perplexity — if the skip fraction is below ~30% or matched-energy perplexity is not strictly better, the idea is dead.

TITLE: Incoherently Sketched Backpropagation with Sparse Gradient Reconstruction

MECHANISM: Per-layer gradients are highly compressible — approximately low-rank across channels and spiky/clustered across token positions — so the backward pass wastes FLOPs measuring a signal with far fewer degrees of freedom than samples. Instead of backpropagating densely, each step draws a *random incoherent* measurement operator (random sign-flipped Hadamard mixing of the residual-stream channels followed by a random k-of-T token-position mask, redrawn per step per layer) and computes only those measurements; the full weight gradient is then recovered by a few iterations of a cheap proximal solver (soft-thresholding in a channel-DCT × token-wavelet basis plus nuclear-norm shrinkage) warm-started from the previous step's gradient estimate. The incoherent mixing is the crux: naive uniform token dropping aliases correlated structure into a biased estimate, whereas random mixing spreads each coordinate's energy across all measurements so a sparsity prior recovers the *unsampled* components rather than discarding them. This helps all three axes simultaneously because backward FLOPs and the activation memory traffic that dominates accelerator energy both drop by the undersampling factor, while the reconstructed gradient stays near-unbiased — so tokens-to-target-loss does not regress, and the freed compute is spent on more unique tokens per step rather than on redundant re-measurement.

TEST: On a 60M-parameter transformer trained for ~1B tokens, plot loss versus measured wall-clock energy (GPU joules) for dense backprop, naive token/channel subsampling, and sketch-plus-reconstruction at 4× undersampling — the idea is falsified if reconstruction fails to beat naive subsampling in gradient cosine similarity to the dense gradient, or if its energy-to-fixed-loss is not below dense at equal or fewer tokens.

text:
TITLE: Reducible-Loss-Gated Token Depth: spend layers only on learnable tokens

MECHANISM: During training, a cheap online reference (an EMA of the model's own earlier checkpoint, or the exit head at layer L/2) scores each token's *reducible* loss — current loss minus reference loss — and only the top-k% of tokens in each batch are propagated through the upper half of the network; the rest terminate at a mid-depth exit head and contribute a cheap auxiliary loss. Because trivially-predictable and irreducibly-noisy tokens are exactly the ones that waste gradient signal, concentrating full-depth forward/backward on high-reducible-loss tokens should raise loss reduction per token seen (data efficiency) *and* per FLOP (compute efficiency) simultaneously, rather than trading them. Energy efficiency comes for free plus extra: the gate is applied as a contiguous compaction (sort-and-pack surviving tokens into dense short sequences before the upper blocks), so the savings are real reductions in HBM traffic and activation-memory writes, which dominate joules per step, not just nominal FLOP counts. The gating fraction k anneals from 100% to ~40% as the reference becomes informative, keeping early optimization stable.

TEST: Train a 150M-param decoder on 6B FiveWeb-Edu tokens against a dense baseline and a random-token-drop control, matched on measured wall-clock GPU-joules, and check whether the gated run is simultaneously better on held-out loss at equal joules *and* at equal unique tokens consumed — if it wins on either axis only by losing the other (or fails to beat random dropping), the idea is dead.

TITLE: Replay epochs in gradient-sketch space, never re-reading data

MECHANISM: During the single pass over the corpus, each microbatch's per-layer gradient is compressed on-the-fly into a rank-1 sketch (mean input activation ⊗ mean output gradient, already materialized in the backward pass) plus a scalar curvature/norm tag, costing ~0.1% of step FLOPs and a few KB per microbatch. These sketches are later re-injected as extra optimizer updates, rescaled by the ratio of current to stored gradient norm on a held-in probe batch to damp staleness — giving the loss-reduction benefit of extra epochs without re-running forward/backward or re-reading tokens. Data efficiency improves because the same tokens yield multiple effective updates; compute efficiency improves because a replayed update costs ~1/1000 of a real step; energy efficiency improves independently because the dominant joule cost at scale is DRAM/NVMe traffic for activations and re-streamed tokens, and a KB-scale sketch replay touches neither. The key bet is that late-training gains from repeated epochs come mostly from low-rank, slowly-rotating gradient directions that a stale sketch still approximates.

TEST: Train a 50M-param model on a fixed 1B-token corpus, comparing 4 true epochs against 1 epoch plus 3 epochs of sketch replay at matched wall-clock, and check whether replay recovers ≥50% of the true-multi-epoch loss gap over the 1-epoch baseline.

TITLE: Phase-Aligned Gradient Routing with Deferral Queues

MECHANISM: Maintain an EMA of the update direction, then score each candidate microbatch by the cosine alignment between its gradient and that direction, estimated cheaply from a last-layer/low-rank sketch computed during the forward pass. Microbatches with strongly negative alignment get no full backward pass; they are pushed to a deferral queue and re-scored later, when the accumulated direction has rotated enough that the same examples now add to progress rather than cancel it. This targets the dominant waste in standard shuffled training — samples whose gradients partially annul the current trajectory, so paid FLOPs yield little net displacement in parameter space — and because rejected samples are re-used rather than discarded, tokens-to-target-loss (data), FLOPs-to-target-loss (compute, since skipped backwards cost ~1/3 of a step), and joules-to-target-loss all fall together instead of trading off. The deferral queue also acts as an implicit hard-example schedule: examples that are destructive early become maximally informative once the model's direction has turned toward them.

TEST: Train a ~150M-parameter model on a fixed token stream and check whether loss-versus-measured-energy strictly improves over both random ordering and a random-skip control matched to the same backward-skip rate; if either control matches it, the alignment signal is doing nothing.

text:
TITLE: Utility-Routed Token Depth: skip layers for already-learned tokens

MECHANISM: During pretraining, a tiny online probe (a linear head on the layer-k hidden state, trained to predict the token's own final-layer loss) scores each token mid-stack; tokens whose predicted loss is already below a running quantile exit early and receive no further forward or backward computation, while high-utility tokens traverse full depth and take a proportionally larger gradient share. Data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on tokens that still carry learnable signal instead of the ~60% of easy, high-frequency tokens that dominate token counts but contribute near-zero gradient norm — this is token-level curation done *inside* training, so no separate filtering pass or discarded corpus is needed. Compute efficiency improves because skipped tokens cost zero FLOPs in the upper layers and zero activation storage, shrinking both forward and backward cost per step rather than just reweighting a fixed-cost step. Energy efficiency improves super-proportionally to FLOPs because early exit removes the corresponding activation writes/reads to HBM, and memory traffic — not arithmetic — dominates joules per token on current accelerators; all three gains come from the same mechanism (removing work on uninformative tokens), so there is no axis being traded.

TEST: Train two ~150M-param models to identical wall-clock energy (measured via on-device power counters) on the same corpus stream — one dense, one utility-routed — and check whether the routed model reaches strictly lower held-out loss at equal joules *and* equal tokens-consumed; if it wins on only one of those two accounting bases, the joint-frontier claim is false.

TITLE: Antithetic batch pairing via free last-layer gradient sketches

MECHANISM: Instead of i.i.d. minibatches, draw a superbatch, compute a near-free 64-dim random projection of each sequence's last-layer gradient (the logit residual outer-product with the final hidden state, already materialized in the forward pass), and greedily match sequences into antithetic pairs whose sketches have maximally negative inner product, then form the batch from those pairs. This is control-variate/antithetic variance reduction rather than diversity or importance sampling: the shared noise directions cancel within each pair while the consistent signal component adds, so the same batch size yields a lower-variance gradient estimate. Since steps-to-target-loss scales with gradient noise relative to signal (critical-batch-size theory), reducing variance at fixed batch size cuts the number of optimizer steps, which simultaneously cuts tokens consumed, FLOPs, and joules — no axis is traded, because the pairing itself costs <0.5% of step FLOPs and touches no extra memory beyond a 64-float vector per sequence.

TEST: Train a 50M-parameter decoder on C4 for a fixed token budget with random versus antithetically-paired batches at identical batch size and schedule, and falsify if measured per-step gradient variance drops less than ~10% or loss-versus-tokens curves are indistinguishable.

TITLE: Function-Preserving Recursive Depth Unfolding with Learned Low-Rank Deltas

MECHANISM: Instead of training a fixed L-layer transformer, train k << L distinct blocks applied recursively (weight-tied loop of depth L), then progressively "unfold" tied positions into independent layers on a pre-planned schedule where each newly independent layer is initialized as its parent plus a learned low-rank delta, making every unfolding step exactly function-preserving so no loss spike or re-warmup is paid. Data efficiency improves because early training updates a shared parameter set with L× the gradient signal per parameter (an implicit ensemble over depth positions), which is known to be the regime where small models are most sample-hungry; the deltas then supply position-specific specialization only where the unfolding schedule says it pays off, chosen by measuring per-position gradient disagreement in the tied state. Compute efficiency improves because most optimizer steps occur while parameter count, optimizer state, and backward-pass weight-gradient work are k/L of final size, while the activation path (and thus representational depth) is full-size from step one. Energy efficiency improves beyond the FLOP reduction because a tied block is reused L/k times per forward pass while resident in on-chip SRAM, raising arithmetic intensity and cutting HBM traffic — the dominant joule cost — so joules/token falls faster than FLOPs/token.

TEST: At ~150M final params, train (a) fixed-depth baseline, (b) standard progressive stacking, (c) the recursive-unfold schedule on identical data, and check whether (c) reaches baseline validation loss at strictly lower tokens, lower total FLOPs, and lower measured wall-clock joules simultaneously — any single axis regressing falsifies it.

text:
TITLE: Score-then-train: fp8 activation-free forwards gate tokens into full backprop

MECHANISM: Each step first runs the *current* model over a 2–3× oversized candidate batch in fp8 with no activation storage and no optimizer state touched (~2ND FLOPs, high arithmetic intensity, minimal HBM traffic), scoring every token by "learnability" = current loss minus an EMA of that token-bucket's past loss, which approximates expected gradient-norm-weighted loss reduction. Only the top-k fraction of sequences (re-packed densely to full context, so no padding waste) receive the real 6ND train step, so total cost is 2N + 6kN versus 6N for standard training — a strict FLOP reduction whenever k < 2/3, while every gradient step is spent on tokens the model can currently still learn from. Data efficiency improves because already-mastered and unlearnable-noise tokens never consume gradient steps; compute efficiency improves because the selection pass is 3× cheaper than a train step and reuses the same weights (no proxy/reference model to train or host); energy efficiency improves super-linearly with the FLOP cut because the skipped work is precisely the activation-store/recompute/optimizer-update traffic that dominates joules-per-FLOP, whereas the added scoring pass is compute-bound and runs near peak efficiency.

TEST: Train a 124M-param model to a fixed 3e18-FLOP budget (measured, including scoring passes) on FineWeb-Edu at k=0.4 versus a random-subset control matched on FLOPs and a full-data control matched on FLOPs, logging wall-clock and GPU energy via NVML; the idea is falsified if validation loss per joule fails to beat both controls.

TITLE: Self-Accelerating Training via Surprisal-Gated Elision of Predictable Spans

MECHANISM: During training, each document's tokens are scored by the model's own cached surprisal from its most recent visit (free, no reference model); contiguous low-surprisal spans are physically deleted from the input sequence and replaced by a single learned "elision" token carrying a cheap hash/length embedding of the removed span, with a small held-out fraction left intact to preserve generation fidelity. Because already-mastered text is removed rather than merely loss-masked, the sequence itself shortens: fewer layer FLOPs, quadratically less attention, and far less KV/activation DRAM traffic — the dominant energy term. Data efficiency improves because every token actually processed carries near-maximal nats of learning signal instead of re-paying full cost for boilerplate. Crucially the effect compounds: as the model learns, more spans become elidable, so cost per corpus-token falls monotonically over the run rather than staying flat.

TEST: At ~150M params, train baseline vs. elision on the same corpus and report held-out perplexity on *uncompressed* text as a function of (a) raw corpus tokens consumed and (b) measured FLOPs/joules — the idea dies if elision fails to dominate the baseline on both curves simultaneously.

TITLE: Affinity-Gated Clonal Adapters with Mastered-Token Compute Suppression

MECHANISM: Replace a fixed dense FFN stack with a small population of low-rank expert modules that are *grown by selection*: during training, each module's per-cluster loss-reduction rate ("affinity") is tracked, and modules with high affinity for a currently high-loss data cluster are duplicated with noise-perturbed copies, while modules whose affinity profiles become redundant or never win routing are pruned, so parameters are allocated only where they measurably buy loss. In the same loop, a running per-token difficulty estimate suppresses backward computation (and, above a threshold, full forward computation via early exit) on tokens already confidently predicted, and the freed budget is spent replaying a small retained buffer of rare high-affinity examples that otherwise appear once. Data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on unmastered and rare tokens instead of the dominant easy mass; compute efficiency improves because both the parameter count and the active FLOPs per token are selected rather than provisioned; energy efficiency improves as a direct consequence, since the same selection signal shrinks activated parameters, skipped token computations, and total steps to target loss simultaneously rather than converting one into another. The key claim is that a single affinity/mastery signal is enough to drive capacity allocation, token-level sparsity, and replay, so the three savings compound instead of competing.

TEST: Train ~150M-parameter models on 3B tokens of a fixed corpus — dense baseline vs. this method with matched *measured joules* — and check whether validation loss (and a rare-fact probe) is lower at equal energy and equal tokens; if it only wins on one axis while degrading another, the compounding claim is false.

TITLE: Early-exit reducible-loss gating: drop uninformative tokens mid-forward

MECHANISM: Attach a lightweight linear LM head to an intermediate layer k (~25% depth) that is trained jointly with a small auxiliary loss. During each forward pass, use this head's per-token loss minus an EMA of its own historical loss for that token's n-gram/context bucket to estimate *reducible* loss; tokens scoring in the bottom p% (already-learned or irreducibly noisy) are masked out of the remaining L−k layers and excluded from the backward pass entirely via sequence repacking. Data efficiency improves because gradient signal concentrates on tokens with genuine headroom rather than high-frequency boilerplate; compute efficiency improves because the dropped tokens cost only k/L of a forward and zero backward (~a 40–50% FLOP cut at p=40% with no extra scoring model); energy efficiency improves superlinearly with the FLOP cut because repacking shrinks activation tensors, reducing HBM traffic and optimizer-state reads, which dominate joules per step. Crucially the gate reuses computation already in the forward pass, so unlike proxy-model data selection or curriculum methods it adds no separate scoring compute to amortize.

TEST: Train a 160M-parameter model on 10B tokens of FineWeb-Edu with p=40% versus an ungated baseline, and check whether it simultaneously beats the baseline at matched tokens (data), matched A100-hours (compute), and matched measured wall-plug joules (energy) on held-out perplexity — failure on any one axis falsifies it.

TITLE: Label-Conditioned Depth Gating with Hard-Token Replay in Saved FLOPs

MECHANISM: During training only, attach a frozen-cost logit-lens readout after every block; because teacher forcing makes the target token known *at the time of the forward pass*, we can gate each token's continued descent through the stack on an oracle criterion (target already ranked top-1 with margin > τ) rather than a learned router, and physically compact surviving tokens into dense ragged batches so skipped work is never executed. The per-step FLOPs freed this way are not banked but immediately re-spent inside the same step on resampled high-surprisal tokens, holding step cost constant while raising the Fisher information carried per FLOP — deep layers see only tokens they can still change, so parameter capacity stops being spent re-deriving already-solved predictions. Compute and energy efficiency improve because loss-per-FLOP and loss-per-joule rise at fixed wall-clock cost per step, with an extra energy win from compaction (dense small GEMMs, higher arithmetic intensity) versus masked sparsity. Data efficiency improves because the oracle gate implicitly reweights the corpus toward unlearned content at zero sampling overhead, so fewer unique tokens are consumed to reach a target loss; at the end, the oracle depth trace is distilled into a small causal router so inference keeps the depth savings without label access.

TEST: Train ~110M-param models on ~2B tokens under three arms — dense baseline, oracle-gated + replay, and random-gated + replay at matched skip rate — and check whether the oracle arm beats baseline on all of loss-vs-unique-tokens, loss-vs-FLOPs, and loss-vs-measured-joules; if it wins only on FLOPs, or fails to separate from the random-gate control, the mechanism is falsified.

TITLE: Alignment-Gated Reflection Steps Against a Slow Weight Trajectory

MECHANISM: Maintain a slow exponential-moving-average replica of the weights alongside the fast optimizer state, as in Lookahead, but replace the usual interpolation-back toward the slow copy with an outward *reflection*: every K steps, set the fast weights to slow + α·(fast − slow) with α ∈ (1, 2], so the fast model's accumulated displacement is amplified along the slow copy's persistent drift direction instead of being damped. The amplification is gated by the cosine between the fast-phase displacement and the slow replica's own recent displacement, applying α > 1 only when the two are aligned (the update is genuinely riding the large-scale descent direction) and falling back to α = 1 otherwise, which prevents the amplified steps from injecting noise in high-curvature regions. Because the gain comes from reusing displacement the optimizer already paid for, each token's gradient is converted into more effective parameter progress (data efficiency), fewer optimizer steps are needed to reach a target loss (compute efficiency), and the per-step overhead is two elementwise vector operations every K steps with no extra forward or backward pass (so wall-clock and joules track the compute saving rather than offsetting it).

TEST: Train a ~150M-parameter decoder on a fixed 5B-token corpus with AdamW, Lookahead, and gated reflection at matched hyperparameter budgets, and check whether gated reflection reaches the AdamW final validation loss with ≥10% fewer tokens and measured wall-clock/GPU-energy; no reduction on any axis falsifies it.

TITLE: Learnability-gated depth truncation using a free EMA reference model

MECHANISM: Maintain an exponential-moving-average copy of the model (already near-free in memory-bound training) and, at each step, score every token by *learnability* = EMA-model surprisal minus current-model surprisal, which estimates remaining reducible loss rather than raw difficulty. Tokens with near-zero or negative learnability are truncated after layer k: they still propagate keys/values upward for context, but their residual stream is frozen, their upper-layer activations are never materialized, and they contribute no gradient. This hits all three axes through one lever rather than a trade: data efficiency improves because gradient budget concentrates on tokens with reducible loss (noise and already-mastered tokens are down-weighted, not just cheapened), compute efficiency improves because upper-layer FLOPs scale with the gated fraction, and energy efficiency improves super-linearly relative to FLOPs because the dominant cost — activation write/read traffic to HBM for the backward pass — is eliminated for gated tokens, not merely reduced.

TEST: Train a 160M-parameter model on 4B tokens of FineWeb-Edu with gating at k=½ depth targeting 50% token retention versus a compute-matched dense baseline, and check whether the gated run reaches equal or lower validation loss at simultaneously fewer tokens, fewer FLOPs, and fewer wall-plug joules (measured via NVML integration) — failure on any one of the three axes falsifies it.

TITLE: Mid-depth activation replay: reuse frozen hidden states as cheap data

MECHANISM: During the normal forward pass, quantize and cache layer-k residual-stream activations (int4, plus a per-token scale) for a sampled subset of sequences, then interleave "replay" steps that inject those cached states directly into layer k+1 and train only the upper stack. Data efficiency improves because each token contributes several upper-layer gradient updates with different neighboring contexts and noise, so fewer unique tokens are needed; compute efficiency improves because a replay step costs only (L−k)/L of forward+backward and skips embedding/tokenization entirely; energy efficiency improves superlinearly because replay batches are pure dense GEMMs over a compact int4 cache resident in HBM, removing the DRAM/disk streaming and long-context attention over the lower stack that dominate joules-per-FLOP. The bet is that lower layers converge to near-stationary feature extractors early, so cached states stay a valid input distribution for a useful staleness window, and drift can be tracked by a cheap periodic recompute probe that adapts the replay ratio.

TEST: Train a ~150M-parameter model for a fixed FLOP budget with replay from k = L/2 versus a standard run, and check whether (a) cosine similarity between replayed and freshly recomputed upper-layer gradients stays above ~0.5 for at least a few hundred steps and (b) replay beats the equal-FLOP, equal-energy baseline on held-out loss; failure of either falsifies it.

TITLE: Quantization noise as the thermal bath for critical-regime pretraining

MECHANISM: Treat the effective gradient/activation noise scale as a temperature and the layerwise feature alignment statistic (e.g., top-eigenvalue fraction of activation covariance, or router occupancy imbalance) as an order parameter; its response to small parameter perturbations — the susceptibility — peaks at a critical noise level where correlations propagate furthest across depth and context, so each token induces the largest coherent structural change per joule dissipated. Instead of paying for that noise with wasted high-precision compute and then re-injecting dropout/LR noise on top, we *source* it from low-precision arithmetic: a controller holds measured susceptibility at its maximum by jointly adjusting mantissa bits (FP4→FP8), LR/batch ratio, and stochastic-rounding seed density, annealing precision upward only as the peak shifts during training. Data efficiency improves because near-critical dynamics maximize information extracted per token (long correlation length = features assembled from distant context rather than memorized locally); compute efficiency improves because fewer optimizer steps are needed to cross each ordering transition; energy efficiency improves independently because the noise is free — it comes from cheap low-bit MACs and reduced memory traffic rather than from extra FLOPs. Crucially the three gains are not traded: precision reduction is *required* by the critical condition rather than tolerated in spite of it.

TEST: Pretrain ~150M-param models at a fixed 3B-token budget across a grid of (mantissa bits × LR/batch ratio), and check whether the run whose measured perturbation-susceptibility is maximal is also the loss minimum — if the susceptibility peak does not coincide with best loss (within noise) at equal tokens, the mechanism is falsified for under a few hundred GPU-hours.

TITLE: Gradient-Surprisal Token Gating for Sparse Backward Passes

MECHANISM: During each forward pass, compute per-token loss and maintain a cheap running estimate of each token's expected gradient contribution (surprisal minus a learned per-position baseline); then run the backward pass only on the top-k fraction (e.g. 30%) of tokens by predicted contribution, masking the rest at the loss level. Because backward is ~2/3 of FLOPs and activation memory is only needed for retained tokens, this cuts compute and energy per step nearly proportionally while keeping every token's forward context intact, so no data is discarded. Data efficiency improves rather than degrades because the retained tokens are exactly the high-information, non-memorized ones, converting the wasted gradient budget spent on trivially predictable tokens into extra effective epochs over hard content. All three axes move together because the saved compute is not reinvested in more steps — the same step count reaches equal or better loss at lower joules, and the reduced activation footprint allows larger batches at fixed hardware.

TEST: Train two 150M-param models on identical 3B-token budgets — dense baseline vs. 30% gradient-gated — and check whether the gated run matches or beats baseline validation loss at strictly lower measured wall-clock and wattage; if its loss is worse at equal tokens, the idea is falsified.

TITLE: Joule-Priced Training: Maximize Nats per Joule per Example

MECHANISM: Instead of a fixed compute budget per token, a small online controller chooses, per microbatch, a *configuration* from a discrete menu that jointly varies three knobs — number of active layers (early-exit backward depth), arithmetic precision, and repetition count — and a tiny value head predicts that config's marginal loss reduction, trained regression-style on observed (config → Δloss) pairs collected for free during training. Each config is priced with *measured* energy from on-device counters (NVML/RAPL), so the controller greedily picks argmax predicted Δnats/Joule rather than argmax Δnats/token, making energy a first-class term in the training objective for the first time. Because expected information gain is the shared numerator across all three ratios, examples that are already learned get routed to shallow/low-precision/single-pass (saving FLOPs and DRAM traffic), while high-signal examples earn extra depth and repeats — improving data efficiency (more learning per token seen), compute efficiency (FLOPs concentrated where gradients are informative), and energy efficiency (the quantity actually being optimized, including memory-movement cost that FLOP proxies ignore). The key unusual claim is that the three axes are *aligned* rather than traded once the allocation is priced in joules, since the dominant waste in standard training is uniform full-cost processing of low-information examples.

TEST: Train a ~100M-param model on ~2B tokens with the joule-priced controller versus a uniform-budget baseline and check whether it wins on final validation loss at *both* matched wall-clock joules *and* matched unique tokens seen — losing either comparison falsifies the alignment claim.

TITLE: Deposition-Grown Networks: Let Gradient Flow Carve Model Capacity

MECHANISM: Invert the assumption that a fixed computation graph is fully instantiated before any data arrives and every token traverses all of it; instead train a narrow trunk and let capacity be *deposited* where residual gradient mass accumulates. Each block maintains a cheap running statistic of per-unit gradient-signal buildup versus carried-through signal; where buildup exceeds a threshold the block splits into parallel sub-branches (new width/expert channels initialized to zero-output so the function is preserved), and branches whose routed token mass falls below a threshold are silted off and pruned, with their parameters recycled into active branches. Because most optimization steps run on a much smaller live subgraph, total training FLOPs and memory traffic (hence joules) fall, while the final parameter count is reached only at the end when it is actually needed. Data efficiency improves because capacity is allocated exactly to the subpopulations of tokens that are still producing irreducible error, rather than being diluted uniformly across a pre-sized dense model that spends early tokens learning where its own capacity should have gone.

TEST: At ~100M final parameters on a fixed 5B-token corpus, train a dense baseline and a deposition-grown run to identical final parameter count, and check whether the grown model reaches equal-or-lower validation loss at both fewer cumulative training FLOPs *and* fewer tokens consumed — failure on either axis falsifies the joint-frontier claim.

TITLE: Per-token selective backpropagation gated by online loss-percentile ranking

MECHANISM: Run the full forward pass as usual, but before the backward pass, rank tokens in the batch by per-token loss against a running per-position/per-frequency baseline and propagate gradients only through the top-k% most "surprising" tokens in the upper transformer blocks (lower blocks still get gradients via the retained tokens' residual stream). Backward is ~2x the cost of forward, so dropping 50-70% of tokens from the upper-block backward cuts total step FLOPs by roughly 30-45% and proportionally cuts DRAM traffic and activation-gradient memory, which is where most joules go on modern accelerators. Because the surviving gradient signal is concentrated on tokens that are not already predictable (boilerplate, copied spans, high-frequency function words), each *observed* token contributes more effective learning signal, so loss-vs-tokens should improve rather than degrade. The gate is a pure training-time change: no architecture modification, no inference-time cost, and it composes with existing data curation since it operates at token granularity where document-level filters cannot reach.

TEST: Train two 150M-param models on identical 4B-token streams — baseline vs. top-40% selective backprop in the upper half of layers — and check whether the selective run reaches equal or lower validation loss at both equal tokens *and* equal measured wall-clock/joules; failure on either axis falsifies it.

TITLE: Gradient-SNR-Matched Per-Weight Precision as an Optimizer State Variable

MECHANISM: Instead of assigning numerical precision by layer or tensor, give every weight its own running estimate of gradient signal-to-noise ratio (cheap: sign-agreement rate and an EMA ratio already implicit in Adam's two moments), and let that SNR dictate how many mantissa bits the weight, its momentum, and its second moment are stored and multiplied in — high-SNR weights are in a deterministic drift regime where the update direction survives 4–6 bits, while low-SNR weights get full precision because there quantization noise aliases directly onto the signal. This is not a uniform-quantization trade: it *removes* stochastic rounding noise precisely where it corrupts learning and tolerates it only where it is dominated by real gradient noise, so loss-per-token should be equal or better, which is the data-efficiency axis. Compute efficiency comes from most weights settling into low-bit matmuls mid-training, and energy efficiency comes disproportionately from optimizer-state DRAM traffic (the dominant joule sink at scale) shrinking with the same schedule, since energy per MAC and per byte moved scales roughly quadratically and linearly in bit width respectively. The SNR field also doubles as a free capacity schedule — precision annealing acts like progressive sharpening of the effective hypothesis class — which is the mechanism by which sample efficiency could *improve* rather than merely hold.

TEST: On a ~100M-parameter model trained for ~2B tokens, inject noise equivalent to 4-bit quantization into only the top-SNR half of weights versus only the bottom-SNR half (matched total noise power, full precision otherwise) — if the two loss curves are indistinguishable, per-weight SNR carries no precision-allocation information and the idea is dead.

TITLE: Pull-Based Token Admission with Early-Exit Rejection for Pretraining

MECHANISM: Replace the static shuffled-corpus pipeline with a small demand-driven buffer (a few thousand sequences) from which the trainer pulls only when the optimizer signals it needs new signal. Every candidate sequence enters the network but is gated at an early layer (say layer 4 of 24) by a cheap learnability head predicting residual loss; sequences below a running quantile threshold are dropped there, so the remaining 80% of the forward/backward FLOPs are never spent on them, and the threshold auto-adjusts to keep the accept rate at the point where marginal loss reduction per joule is maximized. Data efficiency improves because gradient steps concentrate on high-residual-loss, non-redundant text; compute efficiency improves because rejection costs ~1/6 of a full pass instead of a full pass; energy efficiency improves on a third axis because the tiny resident buffer and truncated activations cut DRAM/HBM traffic and activation-memory checkpointing, which dominate joules per step more than FLOPs do. Critically nothing is precomputed by a separate scorer model, so there is no offline data-curation compute debt hidden outside the training run.

TEST: Pretrain a 160M-parameter model on 10B tokens with and without the gate, and check whether the gated run reaches equal validation perplexity at strictly lower values on all three of tokens consumed, total FLOPs, and measured wall-plug joules — any axis that regresses falsifies it.

TITLE: Surprisal-Routed Depth: drop low-signal tokens from deep layers during pretraining

MECHANISM: After the first K transformer blocks, score every token by an online estimate of its learning signal — the running gap between the current model's per-token loss and a cheap frozen n-gram/small-model reference (i.e., reducible surprisal) — and route only the top-p fraction through the remaining blocks, with skipped tokens carried forward by residual identity. Unlike Mixture-of-Depths, which learns an unsupervised router, the score is a direct proxy for expected gradient magnitude, so the dropped compute is compute that would have produced near-zero learning; unlike offline data curation, it operates at token granularity within kept documents, so no data is discarded. Data efficiency improves because per-token gradient budget concentrates on reducible-surprisal tokens instead of memorized boilerplate; compute efficiency improves because deep-layer sequence length shrinks by (1−p), cutting both MLP FLOPs linearly and attention FLOPs quadratically; energy efficiency improves superlinearly relative to FLOPs because shorter deep-layer sequences also shrink KV/activation memory traffic, and DRAM traffic dominates joules per token on modern accelerators. The three axes co-improve rather than trade off because a single mechanism removes work that is simultaneously uninformative (data), expensive (FLOPs), and memory-bound (energy).

TEST: Pretrain three ~150M-param models on identical token streams to a fixed 2e19 FLOP budget — dense baseline, random-drop control at p=0.5, and surprisal-routed at p=0.5 — and check whether surprisal routing beats the dense baseline on held-out loss at equal wall-clock *and* equal measured GPU joules; if it only matches random-drop, the signal-based scoring adds nothing and the claim is dead.

TITLE: Shadow-model gradient control variates for variance-reduced pretraining

MECHANISM: Alongside the main model, carry a ~1%-size frozen "shadow" transformer whose per-example gradient, projected through a fixed random map into the main model's parameter-block statistics, is cheap to compute and whose exact corpus-wide mean is recomputed once per few thousand steps (cost amortized to <1% FLOPs). Each step, subtract the batch's shadow-gradient deviation from the main gradient, yielding an unbiased estimator whose variance is reduced by the shared *data-difficulty* structure (both models see the same easy/hard, repetitive/novel tokens) rather than by shared parameters as in SVRG. Lower gradient variance permits a larger stable learning rate and smaller batch at equal noise scale, so the same loss is reached in fewer optimizer steps *and* fewer tokens — cutting data, FLOPs, and joules together, with the extra win that smaller batches reduce activation-memory DRAM traffic, which dominates energy more than arithmetic does.

TEST: Pretrain a 150M model on 2B tokens with and without the control variate at matched wall-clock, and check whether measured per-step gradient-noise-scale drops by ≥20% and loss-vs-tokens improves; if noise scale is unchanged, the shadow/main gradient correlation is too low and the idea is dead.

TITLE: Feedback-Inhibited Allosteric Gating for Per-Token Compute Conformations

MECHANISM: Each transformer block gets a tiny "regulatory site": a ~0.1%-parameter controller that reads a distal signal — the running surprisal of the model's own recent predictions for that token/context, plus layer-norm statistics — and emits a low-rank multiplicative modulation of the block's FFN and attention weights, switching the block between a cheap "relaxed" conformation (narrow low-rank FFN path, fewer KV reads) and an expensive "tense" one. Crucially the controller sits off the main compute path and never competes with it, so modulation costs almost nothing while reversibly reshaping the catalytic pathway's cost; the surprisal input makes it end-product feedback inhibition, throttling compute on tokens the model has already mastered and releasing full capacity on tokens where loss is still being generated. Data efficiency improves because gradient signal is concentrated on the informative tail of the token distribution rather than smeared across trivially predictable tokens; compute efficiency improves because average FLOPs per token fall while the FLOPs that remain are spent where marginal loss reduction is highest; energy efficiency improves superlinearly to FLOPs because the relaxed conformation reads a strict subset of weights and KV entries, cutting DRAM/HBM traffic, which dominates joules per token. Unlike token dropping or early exit, no token is skipped — every token still receives a forward and backward pass, so the modulation is a reallocation rather than a truncation, which is what lets all three axes move together instead of trading loss for throughput.

TEST: Train a 150M-parameter model on 5B tokens against three matched baselines — dense, random gating at identical average FLOPs, and gating driven by a detached constant instead of surprisal — and check whether the surprisal-gated run strictly dominates on both loss-vs-tokens and loss-vs-measured-joules curves; it is falsified if it fails to beat random gating at matched average FLOPs, since that would show the gain is capacity regularization rather than informative compute allocation.

TITLE: Depth-routing tokens by learning signal for triple-efficiency pretraining

MECHANISM: During pretraining, a cheap online scorer (the model's own layer-k intermediate logits, read via a tied early-exit head) estimates each token's remaining learnable signal; tokens already well-predicted at layer k exit early and contribute only their early-exit loss, while high-signal tokens traverse the full depth and receive full-depth gradients. Because the router reuses existing hidden states rather than a separate scorer model, the selection overhead is <2% FLOPs and requires no extra data passes. Data efficiency improves because the full-capacity gradient budget concentrates on tokens that are actually informative rather than on the ~40% of tokens that are trivially predictable boilerplate; compute efficiency improves because those trivial tokens skip most layers in both forward and backward passes; energy efficiency improves as a direct consequence of fewer FLOPs and fewer activation reads/writes, with no added memory traffic since routing is a within-batch depth mask. Critically this is not a trade: the token-level skipping reduces FLOPs *per token seen*, so at any fixed token budget it is strictly cheaper, and the signal-concentration effect means loss-per-token also improves.

TEST: Pretrain two 150M-parameter models on identical 5B-token streams — baseline vs. depth-routed — and check whether the routed run reaches lower validation loss at *both* equal tokens and equal measured joules (GPU power-meter integrated), falsified if it wins on neither axis or wins on one only by losing the other.

TITLE: Koopman gradient extrapolation: free optimizer steps between real backward passes

MECHANISM: Maintain a rank-r sliding-window Koopman/DMD operator fit online to the last k true gradients projected into a cheap random subspace, then use it to extrapolate the next m gradients and take m optimizer steps that consume neither tokens nor forward/backward passes. Because early- and mid-training gradient fields are dominated by slow, low-frequency directions (the same reason momentum works), these extrapolated steps are near-free descent along the predictable component, while a trust region driven by the measured prediction residual at each recalibration step shrinks m automatically when dynamics become unpredictable. Data efficiency improves because each real token now yields ~(1+m) effective updates without re-fitting that token; compute and energy improve simultaneously because the skipped steps eliminate the full forward+backward FLOPs *and* the dominant HBM activation traffic, and the extrapolation itself is an r×r matrix solve on a projected state. Crucially nothing is traded: the same token budget, fewer FLOPs, fewer joules.

TEST: Train a 50M-param transformer on ~2B tokens with m adaptively ≤4 versus an AdamW baseline, and declare falsified if the method fails to beat baseline loss at *both* matched tokens and matched wall-clock/FLOPs (i.e., if the extrapolated steps merely replicate momentum).

TITLE: Neighbor-Gossip Expert Swarms Replace Global Synchronized Gradient Updates

MECHANISM: Standard training assumes one monolithic parameter set updated by a single globally-synchronized gradient averaged over a shuffled batch; invert this into a population of small models whose only coupling is sparse, asynchronous parameter diffusion toward their k nearest neighbors in a learned specialization-embedding space, with each token routed to its nearest member. Data efficiency improves because a token's gradient concentrates on the sub-population that actually models it rather than being diluted across all parameters, and useful structure still propagates globally through iterated local averaging instead of explicit sharing. Compute efficiency improves because only one small member plus its diffusion partners are active per token, so FLOPs per token fall while total representational capacity stays high. Energy efficiency improves separately from FLOPs because collective communication drops from all-reduce over N devices to k-neighbor exchange, and asynchrony removes straggler barriers, cutting both interconnect energy and idle-but-powered accelerator time.

TEST: At ~150M total parameters and a fixed 3B-token budget, train (a) a dense baseline, (b) a standard top-1 MoE with synchronized all-reduce, and (c) the gossip swarm on identical hardware, and check whether (c) simultaneously beats both on validation loss per token, per training FLOP, and per wall-plug joule measured at the rack — failing any one axis falsifies it.

TITLE: Reference-Free Token Gating with Backward-Pass Repacking

MECHANISM: During the forward pass (which is already required), compute each token's loss and compare it to an EMA of that token's own historical loss plus a running global quantile, yielding a reference-free "learnability" score at zero extra model cost — no auxiliary reference model as in RHO-loss. Tokens scoring below threshold (already-learned or irreducibly noisy) are dropped, and the surviving tokens from several micro-batches are *repacked* into dense sequences before the backward pass, so the skip translates into genuinely fewer backward FLOPs rather than a masked no-op. Data efficiency improves because gradient signal concentrates on high-information tokens; compute efficiency improves because the backward pass (~2/3 of training FLOPs) shrinks proportionally to the drop rate; energy efficiency improves super-linearly with compute because repacking also shrinks activation-gradient HBM traffic and optimizer-step frequency per token consumed, and memory movement dominates joules per FLOP on modern accelerators.

TEST: Train 150M-param models on 4B tokens at matched wall-clock and matched measured joules (nvidia-smi integration) with drop rates {0%, 30%, 50%}, and check whether gated runs reach strictly lower validation loss at *both* equal tokens-seen and equal energy — if any axis regresses versus the 0% baseline, the joint-frontier claim is falsified.

TITLE: Sketch-Decorrelated Multi-Update Steps from Resident Activations

MECHANISM: For each batch, run one forward pass and keep activations resident in on-chip SRAM, then take K≈4 optimizer steps on that same batch, where each step backpropagates through a *different* random low-rank sketch of the weight-gradient subspace (per-step Gaussian projections of the per-layer activation and error matrices), plus a cheap first-order staleness correction applied only to the last block's activations. Because each step sees a decorrelated random view of the loss surface, the K updates are not redundant repeats but approximate K independent-ish descent directions extracted from one token batch, raising learning-per-token (data efficiency). Each sketched backward costs a fraction of a full backward and the forward is amortized K-ways, so FLOPs-per-update drop (compute efficiency). Energy improves more than FLOPs do because HBM traffic — the dominant joule sink — is paid once per K updates rather than once per update, and sketched intermediates fit in SRAM.

TEST: Train a 120M-param decoder on 2B tokens with K=4 versus a token-matched and FLOP-matched baseline, and check whether the K=4 run fails to beat *both* baselines on held-out loss while also drawing fewer measured joules per unit loss reduction.

TITLE: Incoherently Subsampled Backward Passes with Structured Gradient Reconstruction

MECHANISM: Keep the forward pass dense (every token still produces a loss measurement), but run the backward pass only through a variable-density random subset of (token position × layer-block) slots — denser where per-token loss/curvature is high, analogous to sampling the high-energy low-frequency core of a signal more heavily — and never materialize activations for unsampled slots. The resulting measurement set is then used to reconstruct the full dense update by solving a small penalized recovery problem in a low-rank plus temporally-smooth basis (per-step gradients are highly correlated across steps and low-rank across heads/channels, so the true update is compressible and recoverable from far fewer measurements than parameters). Energy-wise this wins twice, because joules per step ≈ α·FLOPs + β·bytes-moved with β/α large on modern accelerators: skipping backward slots removes both the FLOPs and, critically, the HBM activation read/write traffic that checkpointing normally pays for, while reconstruction happens on a tiny coefficient vector resident in SRAM. Data efficiency is not sacrificed because the randomization is incoherent and rotates every step, so all tokens contribute measurements over a short window, and the low-rank projection acts as a denoiser that lowers effective gradient variance per token seen.

TEST: Train two 150M-parameter models on an identical fixed token stream — dense backward versus 25%-density incoherent backward with reconstruction — and check whether the sparse run matches or beats dense on loss-versus-tokens-seen (not just loss-versus-joules); if loss-versus-tokens degrades measurably, it is merely a compute-for-data trade and the claim is false.
